header: **Case and dockets:** Coalition for Economic Equity v. Wilson; Ninth Circuit Nos. 97-15030 and 97-15031; 122 F.3d 692. No separately established Supreme Court docket.

sections.Event: Coalition for Economic Equity v. Wilson; Ninth Circuit Nos. 97-15030 and 97-15031, 122 F.3d 692. Decided November 10, 1998, on review of the Ninth Circuit's vacatur of a preliminary injunction against Proposition 209. The appellate opinion was amended August 21, 1997. The Court considers whether selective removal of authority over race- and sex-conscious measures violates equal protection, whether Title VII preempts that removal, and what preliminary relief is justified. Review proceeds on full merits briefing; no argument date is established. The rehearing writings concern this same proceeding.
sections.Participation: All nine Justices participate: Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer.
sections.Public Action: The judgment is vacated and the case remanded for confined preliminary protection and further proceedings consistent with the separate constitutional and statutory holdings.
sections.Judgment & Remedy:
| Component | Judgment | Vote | Supporting | Opposing |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Racial political-process claim | Reject categorical dismissal; preserve the supported basis for confined preliminary relief | 5-4 | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg, Breyer | O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas |
| Sex theory | Require its own analysis on remand | 5-4 | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg, Breyer | O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas |
| Blanket Title VII preemption | Reject preemption based solely on federal permission for voluntary measures | 9-0 | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer | — |
| Appellate judgment and remedy | Vacate and remand to conform preliminary relief to the supported constitutional injury | 5-4 | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg, Breyer | O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas |

The lower courts must address the supported present burden on ordinary political access to otherwise lawful racial measures while applying the ordinary requirements for preliminary relief and respecting severability. The exact scope of any restraint must follow the actual threatened injury; the Court does not order a particular injunction or automatically reinstate the prior order in its entirety. The discrimination prohibition, unchallenged exceptions and independently lawful operation remain effective to the extent state severability law permits. No particular preference is ordered or permanently validated, and the initiative is not repealed wholesale. The sex theory and any concrete conflict with federal duties require their own adjudication.
sections.Opinion Topology:
| Writing | Author | Joined by | Scope |
|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court, Parts I-IV | Breyer | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Souter and Ginsburg; O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas as to Part III only | Five votes for the constitutional holdings and remedy; all nine for rejection of blanket Title VII preemption |
| Opinion concurring in part and dissenting in part | O'Connor | Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas | Joins Part III; would affirm vacatur of the preliminary injunction on the constitutional grounds |
sections.Holdings:
**Authority:** Breyer's opinion controls Parts I, II and IV with the five votes of Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer. Part III has all nine Justices' support. The following four holdings carry those respective coalitions.

### I. Selective racial restructuring requires a political-process inquiry

**Rule:** A State cannot answer a supported claim that it selectively moved authority over otherwise lawful racial remedies to a more remote political process merely by calling the foreclosed measures preferences. On the district court's preliminary findings, California's removal of those measures to constitutional amendment, while ordinary preferences remain available through ordinary officials, supports confined protection against the resulting unequal political burden; it neither requires a preference nor validates an unconstitutional program.

**Controlling explanation:** Hunter addresses a special political hurdle for racial protection; Seattle applies that principle to selective relocation of decisionmaking over racial remedies even when the underlying measure exceeds federal requirements. Romer preserves that limited doctrine without promising favorable legislation at every governmental level. The district court found both lost opportunities and the special amendment hurdle. Equal words about all races do not dispose of how that allocation operates. Crawford permits withdrawal of a voluntary policy, but does not eliminate Seattle's distinct inquiry into selectively changing who may decide racial questions. The State can enforce the constitutional limits on each proposed program; its interest in preventing unlawful classifications does not alone justify excluding measures that satisfy those limits. Croson, Hopwood and Engineering Contractors continue to require justification and fit. The Court decides the basis for limited preliminary relief, not the permanent validity of every provision or any particular program, and finds no need to attribute animus to voters.

### II. The sex theory requires a distinct inquiry

**Rule:** The racial political-process rule does not by itself resolve a challenge to removing authority over sex-conscious measures. The lower court must examine the asserted sex-based barrier on its own terms, applying the important-objective and substantial-relationship standard to an actual sex classification without presuming that every statewide policy withdrawal creates such a classification.

**Controlling explanation:** Virginia and Engineering Contractors require a genuine important governmental objective and a substantial relationship between that objective and a sex classification; they do not treat a stereotype as justification. Hunter and Seattle concern racial political structure and do not automatically decide every sex-conscious policy. The appellate categorical treatment omitted the separate inquiry. Section 31(c) preserves bona fide sex qualifications reasonably necessary to normal governmental operations in the three covered fields; it is neither a general permission for sex preferences nor proof that the initiative rests on a stereotype. The Court remands the distinct theory without finding all sex-neutrality rules invalid or extending racial strict scrutiny to them.

### III. Federal permission does not establish blanket preemption

**Rule:** Title VII's permission for defined voluntary affirmative action does not alone preempt a State's withdrawal of that policy or guarantee every subordinate governmental entity power to adopt it. An actual conflict with a federal statutory duty or binding federal remedy remains governed by federal supremacy and the applicable savings provisions; no such conflict is decided categorically for every operation of this initiative.

**Controlling explanation:** Weber and Johnson recognize lawful voluntary measures; they do not make every such measure compulsory. Section 703(j) prevents treating numerical imbalance in employment, union membership or related categories, measured against community, geographic or available-workforce figures, as itself requiring preferential treatment. It does not excuse actual unlawful discrimination. Section 708 separately preserves state duties except where state law requires or permits an unlawful employment practice. Section 1104 disclaims occupation of the field and preserves state law unless inconsistent with a provision or purpose of the Civil Rights Act. Those provisions cannot be collapsed into an unlimited exception. Proposition 209 protects existing orders, necessary federal-program eligibility and maximum lawful implementation on its actual terms. The district court's broad statutory theory therefore cannot sustain its entire injunction. Concrete federal conflicts and any distinct question of deference to administrative guidelines remain undecided.

### IV. Preliminary relief must correspond to the supported injury

**Rule:** Interim relief must protect against the demonstrated threatened loss of access to otherwise available lawful racial remedies, while leaving independently lawful provisions operative to the extent severable under state law. The lower court must conform its order to that constitutional injury and the ordinary preliminary-relief requirements, separately resolve the sex theory and concrete federal conflicts, and avoid turning interim protection into a permanent entitlement to a program.

**Controlling explanation:** The district findings supply a present burden on ordinary political access for preliminary consideration, not merely disagreement with an election result. They do not resolve the lawfulness of every affected program, the exact threatened injury defining an injunction's scope, or all remaining equitable prerequisites. The original order extended to implementation insofar as the initiative prohibited or affected affirmative-action programs throughout employment, education and contracting. That formulation may reach beyond the supported injury and does not justify automatic restoration of every part of the order. Section 31(h) requires maximum lawful implementation and severance of an invalid portion. The distinct ban on discrimination, genuine operational qualifications and other independently valid applications must be respected. The Court vacates the appellate judgment that categorically foreclosed the constitutional claim and returns the matter for a fitted order and further proceedings. No injunction validates a program that fails Croson, Hopwood or Engineering Contractors.

**Operative statutory limits:** Section 31 bars governmental discrimination and preferential treatment based on race, sex, color, ethnicity or national origin in public employment, education and contracting. It applies only to action after its effective date. Its sex exception is limited to bona fide qualifications reasonably necessary to normal public employment, education or contracting. It does not invalidate an order or consent decree already in force on the effective date; this protection is not confined to federal decrees and does not automatically extend to every later decree. It preserves action necessary to establish or maintain federal-program eligibility when ineligibility would cost the State federal funds, rather than every federally permitted action. Its governmental coverage includes the State and its local governments, public university systems including the University of California, community-college and school districts, special districts and other political subdivisions or instrumentalities. Remedies are the same regardless of the injured person's race, sex, color, ethnicity or national origin and are those otherwise available under then-existing California antidiscrimination law. The section is self-executing, must operate to the maximum extent federal law and the Constitution permit, and severs an invalid provision from the remainder. These conditions do not themselves establish whether a particular program is lawful.
sections.Precedent Treatment:
- Hunter v. Erickson is applied to the special political hurdle for racial protection; its force does not depend on a right to win a policy dispute.
- Washington v. Seattle School District is applied to selective relocation of racial remedial authority; a voluntary underlying policy is not outside its concern for that reason alone.
- Crawford v. Board of Education is distinguished at its policy-withdrawal scope, which remains effective without erasing Seattle's structural inquiry.
- Romer v. Evans is applied as preserving those racial precedents while rejecting a universal entitlement to favorable law at every governmental level.
- City of Richmond v. J. A. Croson Co. remains the local racial-classification standard; the political-process ruling excuses no defective program.
- Hopwood v. Texas retains its supported educational-diversity justification and required fit; permission does not compel a program.
- Engineering Contractors retains local racial strict scrutiny and the distinct demanding intermediate scrutiny for sex classifications; its limits govern affected measures on remand.
- United States v. Virginia supplies the genuine-objective and substantial-relationship requirement for sex classifications, not an automatic racial political-process rule.
- Adarand Constructors v. Pena retains its distinct federal standard; that standard is not transferred to state or local programs.
- United Steelworkers v. Weber and Johnson v. Transportation Agency are applied as permission for defined voluntary measures, not a universal command or a complete preemption rule.
sections.Law After Decision: The racial political-process rule applies to a supported selective relocation of authority over otherwise lawful remedies despite a substantive preference label. It does not require a program, permanently invalidate every part of Proposition 209, or displace the existing constitutional standards for racial and sex classifications. The sex challenge remains distinct. Title VII permission alone supplies no blanket preemption; concrete federal duties retain their force. Preliminary relief must track the supported injury and preserve severable lawful operation.
sections.Separate Writings: O'Connor, joined by Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas, agrees that voluntary-action permission does not establish blanket Title VII preemption, but would affirm vacatur of the preliminary injunction. The dissent treats Proposition 209 as a statewide substantive restriction on officials' classifications, leaving ordinary antidiscrimination protection available. Crawford preserves the State's choice to withdraw optional policies; lawful remedies under Hopwood and Engineering Contractors are not compulsory policies. Hunter concerned unequal access to ordinary racial protection, and Seattle concerned specially displaced desegregation authority. In the dissent's view, those decisions do not entrench every optional preference-making power at a subordinate governmental level. The reciprocal sex provision likewise does not establish the asserted facial denial of equal protection. This position preserves scrutiny of actual unequal administration, binding federal obligations and properly presented later applications, and does not declare every affirmative measure unconstitutional.
sections.Procedure After Action: The preliminary-injunction appeal returns for conforming relief and further proceedings. The lower courts must distinguish the supported racial structural injury from the unresolved sex theory and concrete statutory conflicts, respect the initiative's actual exceptions and severability, and apply existing standards to any affected program. No final liability judgment, damages award or mandatory preference issues.

header: **Case and dockets:** Pfaff v. Wells Electronics, Inc., No. 97-1130.

sections.Event: **Pfaff v. Wells Electronics, Inc., No. 97-1130.** Argued October 6, 1998; decided November 10, 1998. On review of the Federal Circuit's judgment holding the reviewed patent claims invalid. The question is whether the on-sale bar in then-effective 35 U.S.C. § 102(b) can apply before a working prototype exists when a commercial offer and enabling design already exist.
sections.Participation: All nine Justices participated.
sections.Public Action: The Federal Circuit's invalidity judgment on the reviewed patent claims is affirmed.
sections.Judgment & Remedy:
**Judgment:** Affirmed, 9–0. The Federal Circuit's invalidity judgment remains in effect for the patent claims under review. The Court orders no separate remand, new factfinding, infringement remedy or damages award.

**Supporting:** Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer. **Opposing:** None.
sections.Opinion Topology:
| Writing | Author | Joined by | Scope |
|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court | Scalia | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer | Entire opinion: both cumulative on-sale conditions, their application and all stated limits. |

All nine Justices directly join the entire opinion. There are no separate writings.
sections.Holdings:
### Commercial offer and readiness for patenting

**Operative rule.** The on-sale bar in then-effective 35 U.S.C. § 102(b) applies when, before the date one year before the patent application in the United States, the actual claimed invention is both the subject of a commercial offer for sale in the United States and ready for patenting. Readiness may be shown by reduction to practice or by drawings or descriptions sufficiently specific to enable a person skilled in the art to practice the invention; a working prototype is therefore sufficient but not indispensable.

**Authority.** The opinion of the Court, joined in full by all nine Justices, controls both conditions, their application and the following limits.

**Controlling explanation.** The statute addresses an invention offered for sale, not the manufacture of a first physical specimen. Pennock v. Dialogue supplies the principle that an inventor cannot prolong commercial exploitation and then obtain a later period of exclusivity. The Telephone Cases recognize that an enabling description can establish an operative invention without an indispensable successful prototype. Neither decision supplies a different statutory grace period or itself resolves the present on-sale question.

Both conditions must be proved. A substantial commercial commitment cannot make an incomplete conception ready for patenting, and later successful development cannot retroactively establish readiness before the critical date. Requiring enabling drawings or descriptions of the claimed invention gives that requirement an objective content. An open-ended judgment that development was merely substantially complete is not a substitute.

Here, the Texas Instruments purchase order establishes the commercial commitment, and the engineering drawings were complete enough to permit production before the critical date. The later manufacture of a physical embodiment does not postpone the bar. Pfaff's proposed prototype prerequisite would let the manufacturing schedule extend the period for exploiting an already enabling design.

Mere preliminary negotiations, proposals for future inventive research and incomplete conceptions do not meet the two conditions. Elizabeth v. Pavement Co. preserves the distinction between genuine controlled experimentation and ordinary commercial exploitation. The Court decides no separate experimental-use dispute and invalidates no unidentified claims beyond those under review.
sections.Precedent Treatment:
- **Pennock v. Dialogue, 27 U.S. 1:** Applied for the restriction on prolonged commercial exploitation followed by later exclusivity. Its older statutory setting does not alter the one-year period governing this case.
- **The Telephone Cases, 126 U.S. 1:** Applied for the significance of an enabling description without an indispensable successful prototype; not treated as independently deciding the on-sale trigger.
- **Elizabeth v. Pavement Co., 97 U.S. 126:** Preserved. Genuine controlled experimentation remains distinct from ordinary commercial exploitation; no experimental-use question is separately adjudicated here.
- **Markman v. Westview Instruments:** Its allocation of claim-construction and infringement functions remains intact. It does not itself decide when an invention is on sale.
- **Warner-Jenkinson Co. v. Hilton Davis Chemical Co.:** Its claim-element and prosecution-history rules remain intact. The present inquiry concerns readiness of the actual claimed invention, without changing those rules.
sections.Law After Decision: Courts applying the then-effective on-sale bar must separately determine whether a commercial offer in the United States and enabling readiness existed more than one year before the patent application in the United States. A prototype is one way to establish readiness; enabling drawings or descriptions are another. Neither commercial purpose alone nor later successful development supplies a missing precritical-date condition.
sections.Separate Writings: None.
sections.Procedure After Action: The Federal Circuit's judgment stands for the reviewed patent claims. No additional proceedings are ordered by this decision.

header: **Case and dockets:** Merrill Lynch, Pierce, Fenner & Smith, Inc. v. Kravitz, No. 97-1768.

sections.Event: **Merrill Lynch, Pierce, Fenner & Smith, Inc. v. Kravitz, No. 97-1768.** Decided November 12, 1998. On review of the Third Circuit's en banc judgment reversing summary judgment for the securities firms in consolidated customer litigation. The question is whether firms that execute customer orders at the national best bid and offer despite allegedly better reasonably available terms may be liable for primary fraud under § 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act and Rule 10b-5. No argument date is supplied.
sections.Participation: All nine Justices participated.
sections.Public Action: The Third Circuit's judgment reversing summary judgment is affirmed.
sections.Judgment & Remedy:
**Judgment:** Affirmed, 9–0. The Third Circuit's reversal of summary judgment stands. The customers' claims return for further proceedings on the actual undertaking, reasonably available execution terms, contemporaneous knowledge and all remaining private-action elements. The Court awards no damages, establishes no liability and orders no automatic trial of every issue regardless of ordinary lawful dispositive procedure.

**Supporting:** Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer. **Opposing:** None.
sections.Opinion Topology:
| Writing | Author | Joined by | Scope |
|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court, Parts I-III | Kennedy | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer | Entire opinion: the knowing-deception sufficient ground, application to the disputed execution evidence, preservation of all private-action elements and limited disposition. |
| Opinion concurring | Stone-Zsela | None | Joins the whole Court opinion and judgment; would also recognize reckless materially misleading order acceptance under the existing undertaking, subject to every private-action requirement. |

All nine Justices directly join both controlling holdings. Stone-Zsela's broader recklessness position is stated only in his unjoined concurrence.
sections.Holdings:
The following two holdings are supported by the opinion of the Court and all nine Justices. They resolve the knowing-deception theory and the summary-judgment record. They do not establish a general primary-fraud recklessness rule.

### A knowingly false execution undertaking can be primary securities fraud

**Operative rule.** A broker-dealer that accepts a customer order without price instructions while knowingly intending to disregard the best-execution undertaking it thereby represents can commit primary deception under § 10(b) and Rule 10b-5 when the representation is materially false and the other requirements of a private securities-fraud action are proved. Breach of care or fiduciary duty, inferior execution or the broker's status alone does not establish such fraud; the customer must establish legally sufficient reliance, causation and actual loss as well as the required deception and culpability.

**Controlling explanation.** The parties agreed below that accepting an order without price instructions implies an undertaking consistent with best execution and that acceptance with an intention to breach that undertaking would be a material misrepresentation. Their agreement does not establish what the undertaking required in each transaction or concede any defendant's liability.

First Jersey recognizes a broker's own knowing deception through implied transaction representations. That principle reaches a knowingly false execution undertaking, but First Jersey's proved facts and SEC-enforcement posture do not establish these private customers' reliance, injury or damages. Santa Fe Industries v. Green excludes fiduciary unfairness without deception, and Ernst & Ernst v. Hochfelder excludes negligence. The present theory respects both limits because it requires a false undertaking made with knowledge of its falsity, rather than a later failure to exercise due care.

The securities firms contend that customary execution at the national best bid and offer defined their undertaking and defeated culpability. Such custom is relevant to the actual representation and state of mind. It cannot conclusively immunize an undertaking that the firms understood to be false when made. The customers must prove the representation actually made, including material instructions or disclosed limits, and every other private-action element. A less favorable price creates no presumption of reliance or automatic damage award.

The evidence permits the knowing-deception theory to proceed. The Court therefore does not decide a general primary-liability recklessness standard or transfer Central Bank's separate affirmative-assistance standard to this direct claim.

### The disputed contemporary execution evidence precludes the categorical summary judgment

**Operative rule.** Execution at the national best bid and offer, or through the Small Order Execution System, does not by itself defeat a primary-fraud claim where evidence supports a genuine dispute that better terms were reasonably available and the firm knowingly accepted the order on a false undertaking. Reasonable availability is assessed under contemporary conditions, including order size, the security's trading characteristics, speed, clearing costs and the expense and difficulty of market access, as well as quoted price; later adoption of a rule or development of technology does not itself establish earlier duties, access or culpability.

**Controlling explanation.** The claims concern transactions between November 4, 1992, and November 4, 1994. Customers identify three possible sources of better terms: SelectNet or Instinet quotations, crossing opposing customer market orders, and matching customer orders with in-house limit orders. Expert and industry declarations, evidence of the firms' own use of alternative systems and evidence of particular trades with contemporaneous better quotations support a factual dispute. The firms' evidence of expense, delay and ordinary industry practice supports their defense, but does not conclusively resolve that dispute in their favor.

The relevant question is the best terms reasonably available to the customer. A nominally better quotation need not improve the customer’s execution after practical costs and timing are considered. Conversely, a customary published benchmark is not conclusive when a firm knowingly ignores a feasible improvement inconsistent with its undertaking. Small-order execution through the Small Order Execution System is part of that practical inquiry; the record establishes no universal safe harbor, and not all orders used that system.

This reasoning applies separately to the asserted electronic quotations, crossed market orders and in-house limit orders. It mandates no particular venue, guarantees no best possible price and imposes no universal search of every quotation for every order. Later execution regulations cannot be imposed retroactively on these transactions. A later study of these markets may supply reliable retrospective evidence of contemporary feasibility; adopting a later rule is not itself proof of earlier conditions. Particular-trade evidence supports a real damages controversy, but does not prove injury in every trade, determine class certification or establish reliance, causation or recoverable amounts. The ordinary rules for resolving the remaining issues continue to apply.
sections.Precedent Treatment:
- **Securities and Exchange Commission v. First Jersey Securities, Inc.:** Applied for knowing primary deception through a broker's implied transaction representations. Its established findings and SEC-enforcement posture are distinguished from the disputed facts and private-action elements here.
- **Central Bank of Denver v. First Interstate Bank of Denver:** Its separate culpable-affirmative-assistance route remains intact. Its severe-recklessness standard for that route is not made a general primary-fraud standard, and assistance liability is unnecessary to this disposition.
- **United States v. O'Hagan:** Its requirement of actual deception connected to a securities transaction remains intact. The Court does not extend its distinct source-deception theory to supply the representation here.
- **Santa Fe Industries v. Green, 430 U.S. 462:** Followed. Fiduciary unfairness or breach alone does not constitute federal securities fraud.
- **Ernst & Ernst v. Hochfelder, 425 U.S. 185:** Followed. Negligence is insufficient; the Court does not treat Hochfelder as resolving every primary-liability recklessness question.
- **Basic Inc. v. Levinson:** The requirement of legally sufficient reliance is preserved. A worse execution price supplies no automatic reliance presumption in this case.
sections.Law After Decision: A customer's claim may proceed on evidence of a broker's own knowingly false best-execution undertaking. Neither a published quotation benchmark nor industry custom categorically forecloses that claim. Practical execution circumstances and the full requirements of private fraud remain essential. The Court leaves the broader primary-recklessness question unresolved, and no new execution regulation or automatic price guarantee follows.
sections.Separate Writings:
**Chief Justice Stone-Zsela, concurring; no joins.** The Chief Justice joins the Court's knowing-deception holding and affirmance. He would also hold that reckless, materially misleading acceptance of customer orders under the existing best-execution undertaking can constitute primary § 10(b) and Rule 10b-5 fraud when every ordinary private-action requirement is proved. Acceptance communicates an intention to honor that undertaking; an actionable false representation need not be confined to a defendant's express statement. His broader culpability position goes beyond the sufficient ground the Court adopts and does not become the Court's rule.

He agrees that best execution depends on terms reasonably available under contemporary market conditions, that industry custom informs but does not conclusively resolve culpability, and that later SEC rules cannot create retroactive liability. Later market studies may corroborate evolving feasibility without supplying a retroactive legal command. He would leave knowing or reckless falsity, reliance and actual damage for case-specific proof. Neither breach of fiduciary duty alone, execution at the national best bid and offer nor the existence of a better price automatically establishes fraud, and the concurrence recognizes no reliance presumption from price disparity.
sections.Procedure After Action: The Third Circuit's reversal of summary judgment remains in effect, and the litigation returns for further proceedings consistent with the Court's holdings. The actual undertaking, practical alternatives and contemporary knowledge remain disputed. Reliance, causation, injury, class issues and recoverable amounts remain subject to the applicable law and proof. No compensation or regulatory injunction is ordered, and no automatic trial or favorable merits determination is guaranteed.

Allegations and evidentiary submissions are not merits findings. The reported agreement does not concede liability or every element. The account does not supply a complete set of Supreme Court filings or an argument date. [Hochfelder](https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/425/185) and [Santa Fe](https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/430/462) supply the negligence and deception limits. Later execution rules do not govern the earlier transactions retroactively.

header: **Case and dockets:** Wright v. Universal Maritime Service Corp., No. 97-889; Fourth Circuit No. 96-2850; reported at 525 U.S. 70.

sections.Event:
Wright v. Universal Maritime Service Corp., No. 97-889. Merits decision, November 16, 1998. Argued October 7, 1998. On writ of certiorari to the Fourth Circuit, No. 96-2850, judgment of July 29, 1997, reported at 121 F.3d 702.

Ceasar Wright's ADA action was dismissed without prejudice for failure to pursue the collective grievance procedure, and the Fourth Circuit affirmed. The question is whether the general collective agreement or the separate Longshore Seniority Plan clearly and unmistakably submits his independent federal discrimination claim to arbitration. The Court does not adjudicate the employers' asserted disability-based defense or Wright's discrimination claim.
sections.Participation: All nine Justices participate: Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer.
sections.Public Action: The Fourth Circuit judgment is vacated, and the case is remanded.
sections.Judgment & Remedy:
Vacated and remanded, 9–0. Supporting: Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer.

The exhaustion-based dismissal without prejudice cannot stand on these instruments. The ADA case returns through the Fourth Circuit to the District Court for ordinary proceedings unless another lawful, independently established ground disposes of it. No arbitration or grievance proceeding is compelled.
sections.Opinion Topology:
| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to judgment | Scope joined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court | Breyer | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg | Unanimous Court | Clear-waiver rule, separate CBA and Seniority Plan applications, limits and remand. |

All nine join the opinion in full. No separate writing is filed.
sections.Holdings:
### Neither instrument clearly waives the statutory judicial forum

**Operative rule:** A union-negotiated surrender of an employee's judicial forum for an independent federal discrimination claim must be clear and unmistakable: the agreement must identify that statutory claim or an equivalent class of federal rights rather than merely submit contractual disputes. Neither this CBA nor the separate Seniority Plan does so, and their grievance provisions cannot support dismissal of Wright's ADA action for nonexhaustion; whether a sufficiently explicit collective waiver would be enforceable remains undecided.

**Authority:** The unanimous Opinion of the Court directly adopts the clarity rule, both instrument-specific applications and the bounded remand.

**Controlling explanation:** Gardner-Denver distinguishes an individual's statutory discrimination right from rights created by collective bargaining. Metropolitan Edison requires clarity before a union is understood to waive protected statutory rights. Gilmer involved an individual's agreement to arbitrate a statutory claim; it does not supply missing assent in this collective agreement. AT&T Technologies and First Options require determination of the agreement actually made before invoking arbitral authority. First Options concerns antecedent assent and delegation, not a prior resolution of every collective statutory-forum question.

The employers emphasize that qualification for employment concerns a subject comprehensively covered by the CBA and that its grievance decisions are final. Clause 15(B)'s machinery addresses disputes within the collective relationship. Clause 15(F)'s employment coverage, together with its exclusion of matters outside the agreement, does not expressly incorporate the ADA or submit independent federal claims. Clause 17 prevents the contract from violating law; a legality safeguard is not an agreement to arbitrate every statutory cause of action. Mastrobuono requires reading the actual instrument together, not presuming the broadest imaginable submission.

The Seniority Plan is a separate instrument. Its coverage of disputes about its own terms, interpretation, application and implementing rules likewise identifies no surrender of this ADA forum. The same employment event may give rise to both contractual and statutory questions without merging their sources.

The Court therefore need not decide whether an explicit union-negotiated waiver would be enforceable, resolve general FAA coverage or find the union's alleged advice to sue established. Wright's qualifications, benefits history, discrimination claim and independent defenses remain for the proper court. No ADA violation or entitlement to recovery follows from removal of the grievance-exhaustion bar.
sections.Precedent Treatment:
- Alexander v. Gardner-Denver Co.: applies the distinction between collective contractual rights and the individual's statutory discrimination claim; no categorical decision on explicit waiver enforceability is added.
- Metropolitan Edison Co. v. NLRB: applies the requirement of a clear waiver of protected statutory rights to the forum question presented.
- Gilmer v. Interstate/Johnson Lane Corp.: distinguishes its actual individual statutory-claim agreement; enforceability there does not create assent here.
- AT&T Technologies v. Communications Workers: preserves judicial determination of the submission actually made before arbitration may be compelled.
- First Options of Chicago v. Kaplan (May 22, 1995): applies antecedent assent and independent judicial determination; its arbitrability-delegation rule is not expanded into an already-decided universal collective-waiver rule.
- Mastrobuono v. Shearson Lehman Hutton: applies integrated, instrument-specific construction; no contractual presumption supplies missing statutory-forum language.
sections.Law After Decision: Broad collective grievance language and a contractual legality clause do not alone surrender an employee's forum for an independent federal discrimination claim. Both instruments fail the necessary clarity here. The decision leaves enforceability of an adequately explicit union waiver unresolved and neither disfavors genuinely agreed statutory arbitration nor decides the ADA merits.
sections.Procedure After Action: The action returns through the Fourth Circuit to the District Court without the unsupported grievance-exhaustion dismissal. The dismissal was without prejudice, and the ADA claim and independent defenses remain for ordinary proceedings. No damages, reinstatement, disability-benefit estoppel, grievance or arbitration is ordered. No further Supreme Court event is set.
sections.Source Notes: The [reported objective record, 525 U.S. 70, Part I](https://www.law.cornell.edu/supct/html/97-889.ZO.html), supplies Ceasar Wright's name, the contractual provisions, separate Seniority Plan and procedural history. The union's alleged advice remains Wright's assertion. The Court's disposition concerns contractual scope, not a finding that the asserted disability history establishes or defeats ADA liability.

header: **Case and dockets:** Dodd v. Hood River County, No. 98-54; Ninth Circuit No. 97-35124; 136 F.3d 1219.

sections.Event:
Dodd v. Hood River County, No. 98-54; Ninth Circuit No. 97-35124. Merits decision, November 19, 1998. On writ of certiorari to the Ninth Circuit, 136 F.3d 1219, decided February 13, 1998, affirming summary judgment on the owners' federal takings claims.

The Dodds bought a 40-acre forest-use parcel in 1983 for a retirement home. Oregon proceedings determined that profitable timber use remained. The owners reserved their federal claim and obtained state judicial review. The Ninth Circuit applied issue preclusion narrowly to profitable use and separately rejected the remaining federal grounds; it did not adopt the District Court's equation of the entire state and federal takings inquiries. County authorization to build issued July 1, 1996, leaving the earlier period as the subject of the claimed deprivation.
sections.Participation: All nine Justices participate: Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer.
sections.Public Action: The Ninth Circuit's judgment is affirmed on narrow issue preclusion and the independently stated federal grounds.
sections.Judgment & Remedy:
Affirmed, 8–1. Supporting: Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer. Opposing: Stone-Zsela, who would preserve the narrow preclusion ruling but reserve and remand the federal issues outside the state determination.

All nine directly join the preclusive effect of the necessary, fairly litigated finding of profitable timber use. That agreement concerns a legal premise within this single judgment; it does not separately dispose of the federal cause or establish a precise residual valuation. Eight Justices join the independent federal grounds sustaining the judgment.

No new permit, compensation award or jury trial is ordered. The July 1996 permission limits duration; it does not itself erase an earlier taking.
sections.Opinion Topology:
| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to judgment | Scope joined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court, Part I | Stevens | Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer | Unanimous preclusion proposition; Stone opposes the final affirmance | Lawful Oregon effect, actual requirements and the limited profitable-use finding. |
| Opinion of the Court, Parts II–IV | Stevens | O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer | Court, eight; complete affirmance | Independent federal merits, actual duration and resulting denial of further relief. |
| Opinion concurring in part and dissenting in part | Stone-Zsela | No other Justice joins | Joins Part I; would remand the remaining federal issues | Preclusion's limits and express reservation of federal questions outside the Oregon determination. |

All eight Associate Justices join the entire Court opinion. Stone-Zsela joins Part I only and does not join Parts II–IV's federal merits grounds.
sections.Holdings:
### I. Reservation of the federal cause does not erase a necessary, fairly litigated state finding

**Operative rule:** Section 1738 gives the Oregon judicial determination its lawful state preclusive effect: reserving a federal takings cause does not exempt an identical factual issue actually and necessarily litigated with a full and fair opportunity by parties bound in proceedings Oregon recognizes. Those requirements establish preclusion of profitable timber use here, but not of the entire federal claim, every federal element, a precise residual valuation or the legal assessment of partial deprivation.

**Authority:** Part I of the Court's opinion has all nine Justices' direct support.

**Controlling explanation:** Baker requires lawful rendering-state effect without a general public-policy exception; Allen applies that principle to actually litigated issues. England preserves federal questions following federal abstention, not a unilateral right to contradict a necessary finding in separate state compensation litigation. Williamson County's then-governing compensation requirement does not create the claimed exemption, and the Dodds completed the state process. Richards requires lawful authority to bind and adequate opportunity; these owners were actual parties.

Each Oregon condition is satisfied at the proper level of specificity. The existence of profitable timber use is the same factual issue relevant to total federal deprivation. The competing appraisal and forester evidence were presented, and the use finding was necessary to the final state no-taking determination. Available evidentiary procedures, including a hearing available on request and witness examination, together with actual presentation and judicial review, supplied a full and fair opportunity. The Dodds themselves were parties. The LUBA adjudication and ensuing judicial review are proceedings Oregon recognizes for this purpose. The reported failure to request the available hearing does not eliminate the opportunity; Kremer distinguishes adequacy from use of every available procedure.

The federal cause remains distinct. The state finding establishes retained profitable use, not the federal significance of every restriction or a particular dollar value. The Court therefore rejects complete preclusion and separately addresses the federal grounds. No rule makes every administrative proceeding fair or every reserved federal issue precluded.

### II. Profitable timber use defeats only the complete-deprivation category

**Operative rule:** The binding finding that this parcel retains profitable timber use defeats a Lucas claim that the restriction eliminated all economically beneficial use. It does not itself decide partial deprivation under Penn Central, and no background-property limitation need be found when the necessary complete loss has not been established.

**Authority:** Part II has the eight Associate Justices' direct support; Stone-Zsela does not join this federal merits determination.

**Controlling explanation:** Lucas supplies a categorical compensation rule after complete deprivation, subject to a substantiated antecedent property or nuisance limitation. Profitable timber use prevents the owners from establishing that categorical premise. The Court need not decide that Oregon's Goal 4 restriction already excluded the proposed dwelling from title or shift Lucas's background-law burden before total deprivation is shown. Prior enactment or a legislative description of harm would not alone satisfy that burden in a case that reached it. Del Monte Dunes preserves the separate partial-taking inquiry; the failure of the total-loss category does not end that inquiry here.

### III. The independent contextual federal inquiry supports this summary judgment

**Operative rule:** A partial-taking claim requires consideration together of economic impact, reasonable investment-backed expectations and the character of governmental action; retained value, acquisition under an existing restriction or a legitimate regulatory objective alone is not dispositive. On this undisputed record, continued profitable timber use, the existing necessary-and-accessory dwelling condition, nonassuring County communications and the forest-management character of the restriction support rejection of the claim; the restriction also bears the required relationship to the specified forestry purposes under the received Agins inquiry, without a demanded conveyance triggering Dolan.

**Authority:** Part III has the eight Associate Justices' direct support, including its distinct contextual and purpose-relationship applications; Stone-Zsela does not join those merits grounds.

**Controlling explanation:** Penn Central requires the combined inquiry, not an equation between any remaining use and constitutional validity. The property continued to support profitable timber production. The claimed retirement dwelling was subject at acquisition to an existing statewide requirement that it be necessary and accessory to forest use. County communications did not promise the required permits. Those facts bear on the reasonableness of this particular expectation; they do not establish that later purchasers lose constitutional protection.

The regulation restricts forest use to serve actual forestry, fire-protection and chemical-application objectives. It neither occupies the parcel physically nor demands a property conveyance. Its actual relationship to those purposes satisfies the received Agins inquiry at the bounded scope preserved in Del Monte Dunes. Dolan's special nexus-and-proportionality burden for a demanded conveyance therefore does not govern.

The owners correctly distinguish their federal cause from the narrower Oregon finding and insist that retained use alone cannot answer their claim. The Court addresses the remaining legal restriction, actual communications, continuing use and governmental character independently. It neither fixes a percentage diminution nor calls an unknown loss trivial. The reported undisputed record supplies no material factual conflict requiring another trial under the governing standards. Del Monte Dunes protects a properly supported factual taking claim while retaining judicial sufficiency review; it does not guarantee a trial on a precluded fact or unsupported dispute. Personal residential plans receive ordinary property protection, and the result does not depend on labeling them noncommercial.

### IV. Later permission limits the claimed duration without curing a prior taking

**Operative rule:** The July 1, 1996 building authorization ends treatment of this dispute as an ongoing prohibition but does not itself defeat compensation for an earlier proved taking. Because the independently considered total- and partial-taking grounds establish no antecedent violation here, the actual-period claim supplies no compensation or basis for new factfinding.

**Authority:** Part IV has the eight Associate Justices' direct support; Stone-Zsela would reserve and remand the federal issues rather than join this final resolution.

**Controlling explanation:** First English, Lucas and Del Monte Dunes preserve compensation for the attributable duration of an actual taking. Permission issued later does not make an earlier unconstitutional deprivation disappear. Equally, delay in permission does not establish the antecedent violation without the substantive inquiry. That inquiry has been resolved against the owners on the stated record. The Court therefore awards no compensation, orders no new permit and requires no additional factfinding. Criticism of how quickly the owners pursued development supplies no constitutional forfeiture rule.
sections.Precedent Treatment:
- Baker v. General Motors Corp. (January 13, 1998): applies its unanimous lawful-recognition component, not its distinct testimony-process application.
- Allen v. McCurry: applies ordinary issue preclusion to an actually litigated state determination; the entire federal cause is not equated with the state claim.
- Kremer v. Chemical Construction Corp.: preserves the distinction between an adequate available opportunity and failure to employ every procedure.
- Richards v. Jefferson County: preserves constitutional authority to bind and fair opportunity; these participating owners differ from absent litigants without a sufficient binding relationship.
- England v. Louisiana State Board of Medical Examiners: preserves federal questions after abstention without creating a unilateral exemption for necessary findings from separate state proceedings.
- Williamson County Regional Planning Commission v. Hamilton Bank: retains its then-effective compensation prerequisite at the boundaries preserved in Del Monte Dunes; no new ripeness rule is adopted.
- Lucas v. South Carolina Coastal Council: applies complete-deprivation requirements and preserves the conditional background-law burden and distinct partial-taking analysis.
- Penn Central Transportation Co. v. New York City: applies the combined economic-impact, expectations and governmental-character inquiry; no single-factor shortcut is adopted.
- Del Monte Dunes at Monterey, Ltd. v. City of Monterey (June 16, 1997): preserves the total/partial distinction, actual-period compensation, bounded purpose-relationship inquiry and ordinary judicial sufficiency review alongside its jury rule.
- Agins v. City of Tiburon: applies the received relationship inquiry only to this restriction's stated forest-management purposes, without a comprehensive new substantial-advancement formulation.
- Dolan v. City of Tigard: distinguishes its demanded-conveyance nexus-and-proportionality burden; no such exaction is present here.
- First English Evangelical Lutheran Church v. County of Los Angeles: preserves compensation for a proved taking's actual duration; later permission is not a retrospective cure.
sections.Law After Decision: A federal-claim reservation preserves questions outside the actual state adjudication but does not erase the ordinary preclusive effect of necessary, fairly litigated common facts. Here profitable timber use binds the owners and defeats complete deprivation. The distinct federal partial-taking and purpose-relationship inquiries are independently resolved on the actual record; continued use alone does not decide them. Later permitting limits duration without automatically defeating a temporary-taking claim. No compensation, universal notice-at-purchase bar or special disability for residential plans is created.
sections.Separate Writings:
Stone-Zsela concurs in Part I and dissents from final resolution of the remaining federal issues. He agrees that §1738 governs the lawful effect of matters actually, necessarily and fairly decided in Oregon and that a federal reservation cannot erase the binding profitable-use finding. He also agrees that the whole federal cause and its unadjudicated elements are not precluded merely because state takings litigation occurred.

He would preserve that narrow preclusion and return the federal questions outside the state determination for adjudication. He does not join the Court's independent conclusions under Lucas, Penn Central, the purpose-relationship inquiry or the actual-period claim. His position neither finds a taking nor directs compensation, a permit or a jury trial, and it does not announce a separate substantive takings rule. The disagreement concerns final adjudication of those federal issues in this disposition after recognizing the limited state effect.
sections.Procedure After Action: The Ninth Circuit judgment stands on the confined preclusion ruling and independently stated federal grounds. Supreme Court review is complete. No compensation, new permit, additional trial or further factfinding is ordered, and no further Supreme Court event is set.
sections.Source Notes: The complete [Ninth Circuit opinion, 136 F.3d 1219](https://openjurist.org/136/f3d/1219), including its preclusion and independent federal-merits discussions, supplies the state proceedings, available evidentiary procedures, actual County communications, remaining timber use and July 1, 1996 authorization. The binding finding concerns profitable use, not a newly fixed residual valuation. Reported procedural choices are distinguished from gaps in research; residential purpose and development pace are not constitutional disqualifications. The review question is an issue statement, not a quotation from the grant.

header: **Case and dockets:** Wisconsin Right to Life, Inc. v. Paradise, No. 98-118; Seventh Circuit No. 97-3668.

sections.Event:
Wisconsin Right to Life, Inc. v. Paradise, No. 98-118. Merits decision, November 24, 1998. On writ of certiorari to the United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit, 138 F.3d 1183, No. 97-3668. The appellate opinion issued March 13, 1998; rehearing was denied April 16. The matter was submitted for merits review.

The question is whether WRTL may pursue its pre-enforcement challenge to Wisconsin political-committee registration and enforcement provisions under Article III. The District Court found standing but abstained under Railroad Commission v. Pullman Co.; the Seventh Circuit vacated and directed jurisdictional dismissal. WRTL sought facial invalidity and nonenforcement, while the officials disputed credible threatened injury and the ability of relief against them to address independent private suits.
sections.Participation: All nine Justices participate: Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer.
sections.Public Action: The Seventh Circuit's judgment is vacated, and the case is remanded for further proceedings consistent with the Court's opinion.
sections.Judgment & Remedy:
Vacated and remanded, 7–2. Supporting: Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer. Opposing: Scalia and Thomas, who would affirm the direction to dismiss without prejudice for want of jurisdiction.

The remand requires consideration of the actual claims, threatened personal injury, proper defendants and proposed relief. It neither affirms the District Court's standing finding nor decides whether Pullman abstention was warranted. No Wisconsin provision is invalidated and no injunction issues.
