The [filed petition, opposition and lower appendices](https://archive.org/details/micro_IA40386003_1052) supply the lower judgments and procedural posture. The governing statutory texts are [35 U.S.C. §101](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-1994-title35/pdf/USCODE-1994-title35-partII-chap10-sec101.pdf) and [§112](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-1994-title35/pdf/USCODE-1994-title35-partII-chap11-sec112.pdf). No argument date or separate Supreme Court docket is stated in the supplied chronology.

header: **Case and dockets:** California Public Employees' Retirement System and Florida State Board of Administration v. Paul Felzen et al., No. 97-1732.

sections.Event: California Public Employees' Retirement System and Florida State Board of Administration v. Paul Felzen et al., No. 97-1732. Argued January 11, 1999; decided January 20, 1999. On writ of certiorari to the Seventh Circuit, Felzen v. Andreas, 134 F.3d 873 (January 21, 1998). The question is whether shareholders who respond to Rule 23.1 notice, appear and object to approval of a derivative settlement must intervene to appeal. Both institutions were heard in opposition to the settlement but chose not to seek intervention. The District Court approved the settlement on July 7, 1997; their July 14 notice of appeal identified the settlement judgment and fee/expense order. The Court of Appeals dismissed on the appellate-status ground without reaching the settlement's merits.
sections.Participation: All nine Justices participated at argument and decision.
sections.Public Action: The judgment dismissing the institutions' appeal is affirmed.
sections.Judgment & Remedy: **Affirmed, 5–4.** Supporting: Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas. Opposing: Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer. The dismissal leaves the settlement undisturbed because this attempted nonparty appeal cannot proceed; the Court does not approve the settlement's substantive fairness or decide attorney compensation. No intervention application, denial, reopening, tolling or late-intervention entitlement is adjudicated. The dissent would reverse the status dismissal and remand for further appellate proceedings under a limited representative-objector rule, without directing rejection of the settlement or granting fee relief.
sections.Opinion Topology:
| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to judgment | Scope joined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court | Stone-Zsela | O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas | Affirms dismissal | Both holdings, their complete reasoning, qualifications and confined remedy. |
| Dissent | Stevens | Souter, Ginsburg, Breyer | Would reverse and remand | Limited representative-objector status for review of the rejected settlement objections; no settlement or fee merits determination. |
sections.Holdings:
#### 1. Rule 23.1 objection does not itself confer the party status needed for this appeal

**Holding and operative rule:** A shareholder who is otherwise not a party does not acquire appellate party status merely by appearing under Rule 23.1 notice and presenting objections that the district court hears and rejects when approving a derivative settlement. To appeal that settlement judgment, the shareholder must properly become a party through intervention; shareholder interest, notice and the recognized opportunity to object do not themselves supply the necessary status.

**Authority:** Stone-Zsela's opinion of the Court is joined by the other four members of the coalition comprising Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas. All five adopt both holdings and their stated qualifications.

**Controlling explanation:** The Court holds that an opportunity to assist the settlement court by objecting is distinct from authority to continue the corporate litigation on appeal. Marino v. Ortiz supplies both the general party-status rule and its application to persons actually heard in opposition to a settlement who had not intervened. Rule 23.1 recognizes shareholder participation in the district court's supervision of the corporate claim; that function does not itself confer the separate appellate role. Tryforos v. Icarian Development Co. supplies the strongest contrary rule. Its distinction between objecting to disposition and assuming prosecution expressly included an appeal by a shareholder who appeared to oppose a proposed settlement. The Court rejects that settlement-appeal proposition insofar as it permits this appeal without intervention: limiting an objector's appellate objectives does not remove the status prerequisite Marino applies. Izumi Seimitsu Kogyo Kabushiki Kaisha v. U.S. Philips Corp. reinforces the distinction between interest and status, although its undisturbed intervention denial and separately unpresented intervention question differ from this case's direct status challenge. Johnson v. Manhattan Railway Co. does not establish an independent route here. Its discussion of invitation, appearance and appeal at page 495 is followed at page 496 by an explanation why the applicable equity rule would not obstruct intervention, in a distinct receivership setting. Neither passage decides modern derivative-objector status by itself. These institutions were heard but sought no intervention. Their reliance on earlier circuit practice does not constitute admission as parties, and no denial of an application is before the Court.

**Limits:** This is a rule for the presented derivative-settlement appeal, not a categorical prohibition of every nonparty appeal under every procedural regime. Section 1291 supplies the final-decision framework, Appellate Rule 3(c) concerns identification of appellants, Rule 23.1 governs the recognized objection role, and Rule 24 supplies intervention; neither §1291 nor Rule 3(c) is treated as expressly deciding every party-status category. The decision rests on actual participation and the absence of intervention, not on a finding that the institutions violated a notice or service condition.

#### 2. Intervention review and nonparty due-process protection remain distinct

**Holding and operative rule:** Requiring intervention for this settlement appeal does not foreclose review by an actual party or an appropriate appeal from an actual denial of intervention. Nor does it impose a general duty to intervene in another person's suit to preserve an otherwise independent claim: constitutional limits on binding genuinely unrepresented persons remain, without establishing an appellate entitlement or a collateral remedy in this case.

**Authority:** The same five-Justice opinion of the Court controls this boundary and the confined affirmance.

**Controlling explanation:** Izumi preserves a lawful route for reviewing an intervention denial while distinguishing it from review of the underlying judgment by a party. No such denial exists here, so the Court decides neither entitlement to intervention nor the timing or result of an application never made. Richards v. Jefferson County protects a person's own rights against preclusion without constitutionally sufficient consent, control, genuine privity, adequate representative litigation or another recognized basis consistent with due process. Its rule does not make every affected person an appellate party. Matsushita Electric Industrial Co. v. Epstein preserves the independent requirement of adequate representation; notice, opportunities to object or opt out do not cure its constitutional absence. Those protections remain effective, but neither adequate nor inadequate representation is established by the derivative label or by these institutions' appearance. The claim settled below belongs to the corporation, while Richards involved direct personal claims. Keeping that distinction does not decide whether any particular independent shareholder claim exists or may proceed. The status ruling accordingly leaves the settlement's fairness, compensation terms and any properly presented intervention or due-process question undecided.

**Questions not reached and remedial limits:** The Court orders no reopening, tolling, late intervention, new hearing, discovery or review of a fictional denied motion. It does not independently decide the petition's requested pure-prospectivity question or adopt the Court of Appeals' broader assertion that every possible operation of Chevron Oil was eliminated. Harper's rule against selective prospectivity after application of a federal rule to the Court's litigants remains at its established scope; it creates no unsupported transition entitlement here. No settlement-fairness, fee-merits, collusion, representation-adequacy, personal-claim or collateral-preclusion judgment follows.
sections.Precedent Treatment:
- **Marino v. Ortiz, 484 U.S. 301:** Applied to the distinction between being heard as a settlement objector and properly obtaining party status for appeal. Its separate equally divided collateral-action disposition supplies no general preclusion rule here.
- **Tryforos v. Icarian Development Co., 518 F.2d 1258, Part I and footnote 22:** Its express route for an appearing Rule 23.1 shareholder to appeal a proposed settlement without intervention is rejected to the extent inconsistent with today's rule. Its separate service, notice-of-appeal and fee rulings are not adjudicated or displaced merely by that conclusion.
- **Izumi Seimitsu Kogyo Kabushiki Kaisha v. U.S. Philips Corp. (November 30, 1993):** Its party-status boundary and route to review an actual intervention denial are applied; its different §1254(1), denied-intervention and question-presentation posture is preserved. It is not treated as having already decided the specific Rule 23.1 route presented here.
- **Johnson v. Manhattan Railway Co., 289 U.S. 479, 495–496:** Its invitation/appearance discussion and adjacent intervention analysis are read together in their receivership context. It establishes neither an unqualified modern nonparty-appeal right nor, by itself, a universal formal-motion requirement.
- **Richards v. Jefferson County (June 10, 1996):** Its protection of independent rights against unsupported nonparty preclusion remains intact. It supplies no automatic appellate status and no general duty to intervene to preserve an independent claim.
- **Matsushita Electric Industrial Co. v. Epstein (February 27, 1996):** Its adequate-representation component remains distinct from notice and objection opportunities. No broader collateral-review question is resolved.
- **Harper v. Virginia Department of Taxation (June 18, 1993):** Its applied-rule prohibition on selective prospectivity retains its actual scope. The Court does not adopt a blanket disposition of all prospective rulings or every possible Chevron Oil question.
sections.Law After Decision: Rule 23.1 continues to protect the opportunity to object to disposition of a derivative action, but an otherwise nonparty shareholder must use the intervention route to obtain the party status required for this settlement appeal. The contrary settlement-appeal proposition in Tryforos no longer governs this setting. Actual-party review and review of a genuine intervention denial remain distinct lawful routes. The decision neither converts notice into constitutionally adequate representation nor weakens the protection of independent rights against unsupported nonparty preclusion. It leaves the settlement undisturbed without deciding its merits or creating a new intervention or collateral proceeding.
sections.Separate Writings:
**Justice Stevens, joined by Justices Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer, dissenting.** The dissent would recognize a confined appellate role for a shareholder who responds to the Rule 23.1 settlement notice, appears, presents objections, and has those objections heard and rejected in the disposition of the corporate claim. The procedural role, rather than mere ownership, financial exposure, receipt of notice or potential binding effect, supplies status to seek review of that disposition. It does not make the objector a plaintiff controlling prosecution or give a nonappearing shareholder a right to appeal.

Tryforos, which Justice Stevens authored as a circuit judge, supplies the direct distinction between objecting to disposition and undertaking prosecution. Its footnote expressly includes proposed settlements, although the actual objection there concerned dismissal with prejudice and the corporation's lack of service. Marino presents a serious contrary example because its objectors were heard too. The dissent distinguishes their adverse personal interests in another action from the Rule 23.1 shareholder's defined role concerning disposition of the represented corporate claim. Izumi involved an undisturbed intervention denial and a different presented question; it does not foreclose deciding that this recognized role supplies limited status. Johnson offers an equity analogy linking invitation, appearance, objection and appeal, but its adjacent intervention discussion and receivership setting prevent treating it as a universal nonintervention rule. Richards protects independent nonparty rights without itself creating appellate status.

The dissent would reverse only the status dismissal and remand for further appellate proceedings subject to ordinary preservation and appeal requirements. It would not invalidate the settlement, find collusion or inadequate representation, permit new claims, promise success on the objections or establish reviewability or entitlement on every fee contention. It proposes no independent prospective-only ruling, reopening, tolling or automatic late intervention. Its limited representative-objector rule does not control the judgment.
sections.Procedure After Action: The Seventh Circuit's dismissal stands. The settlement remains undisturbed as a consequence of that dismissal, without a Supreme Court determination of its substantive fairness or fee terms. No case is remanded for merits review, and no intervention application or other proceeding is ordered or deemed pending. An appropriate actual-party appeal or review of an actual intervention denial remains governed by its own lawful requirements.
sections.Source Notes: [The Seventh Circuit opinion](https://law.resource.org/pub/us/case/reporter/F3/134/134.F3d.873.97-2829.html) supplies the status dismissal and the objectors' decision not to intervene. The original petition caption and Rule 23.1 notice, preliminary order, hearing and appeal excerpts identify both institutional petitioners, the invitation to object, their actual appearance and the dated orders. The notice's settlement descriptions and the District Court's fairness findings are not adopted here as Supreme Court findings. [Tryforos's primary court transcription](https://static.case.law/f2d/518/cases/1258-01.json), the [official Marino report](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-484/pdf/USREPORTS-484-301.pdf), and the [official Johnson report](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-289/pdf/USREPORTS-289-479.pdf) support the distinct procedural routes and limits discussed. No determination rests on disputed exact waiver wording, an unreported ruling in the hearing's omitted middle, or an unestablished intervention application.

header: **Case and dockets:** Department of the Army v. Blue Fox, Inc.; No. 97-1642; OT1998.

sections.Event:
**Department of the Army v. Blue Fox, Inc., No. 97-1642.** Argued December 1, 1998; decided January 20, 1999. On writ of certiorari to the Ninth Circuit, 121 F.3d 1357, which permitted an equitable-lien claim against the Army. The question is whether APA §702 waives immunity for that remedy. The separately rejected SBA claim is outside review.

The Army obtained no Miller Act payment or performance bond for Verdan's contract. Blue Fox remained unpaid $46,586.14; after notice of the debt the Army paid Verdan $86,132.33. The later $84,910.52 project balance partly financed the $126,772.78 replacement contract. No earned Verdan balance remains withheld. Blue Fox limits its claimed lien to contract funds and argues that notice and its suit prevented subsequent disbursements from extinguishing the asserted charge.
sections.Participation: All nine Justices participated at argument and decision.
sections.Public Action: The Ninth Circuit's judgment permitting the Army lien claim is reversed, and the case is remanded with instructions to dismiss that claim for lack of an applicable waiver of sovereign immunity.
sections.Judgment & Remedy:
**Reversed and remanded, 9–0.**

**Supporting:** Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer.

The Army lien claim must be dismissed. The Court orders no payment, recreated project balance, replacement lien or tracing hearing. The SBA judgment is untouched. A properly founded alternative remedy remains subject to its own governing law; no existing surety recovery or direct Tucker Act entitlement is established here.
sections.Opinion Topology:
| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to judgment | Scope joined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court | Scalia | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer | Reversal and remand for dismissal of the Army lien claim | Full waiver rule, actual-remedy application and every stated reservation. |

All nine join; no separate writing is filed.
sections.Holdings:
#### The requested lien supplies substitute compensation without an applicable waiver

**Operative rule.** Section 702 does not waive federal immunity for an equitable lien whose function is substitute payment from Government property for a private debtor's default when no identified retained property belonging to the claimant or specific statutory payment entitlement supports the requested recovery. The equitable form and identification of a project account do not establish consent; specific enforcement of an actual entitlement remains a different question under its own governing law.

**Authority.** Scalia's Opinion of the Court has all nine Justices' direct joins and controls the rule, application and limits.

**Controlling explanation.** Section 702's waiver excludes money damages. Bowen distinguishes substitute compensation from specific relief enforcing an actual entitlement, including a statutory entitlement to payment; it does not classify all monetary relief as damages. Nordic Village and Lane separately require consent to the remedy actually sought. A substantive duty, general jurisdiction or equitable description cannot supply missing consent.

Blue Fox expressly seeks contract funds and argues that its lien attached at notice, making later disbursements ineffective against it. But that attachment is the legal proposition to be established, not an accepted finding that the Army retained Blue Fox's property. No earned Verdan payment remains withheld, and the distinct completion balance is not shown to belong to Blue Fox. The requested recovery would replace Verdan's unpaid debt from Government property. Calling the Army a stakeholder cannot establish both the underlying entitlement and consent to that substitute obligation.

Henningsen and Pearlman concern surety or subrogation rights; Munsey Trust likewise supplies no general direct subcontractor right to recover against the Army free of immunity. The Miller Act's bond protection does not make the Government a guarantor when it fails to obtain the required bond. No bond exists here, and the Government's administration does not itself enact a payment mandate or waiver. That failure is not approved; it simply does not supply consent.

Immunity resolves this claim before independent equitable merits. The Court does not declare every equitable lien money damages or decide a genuine proceeding for claimant property under applicable authority. It also leaves the disputed agency-action, reviewability and adequate-remedy arguments under §§702 and 704, and the related preservation objection, unanswered. The money-damages limitation is sufficient.
sections.Precedent Treatment:
- **Bowen v. Massachusetts, 487 U.S. 879:** Preserved and distinguished. Its specific statutory payment entitlement differs from compensation for this private debt; money alone is not the classification rule.
- **United States v. Nordic Village, Inc.:** Applied to require consent for the particular affirmative recovery and to reject equitable or property labels as substitutes. Genuine identified-property proceedings retain their own facts and authority.
- **Lane v. Peña:** Applied to separate a substantive governmental duty from waiver of immunity for the actual monetary remedy.
- **Henningsen v. United States Fidelity & Guaranty Co., 208 U.S. 404:** Distinguished as a surety/subrogation setting; it supplies no direct Army waiver for this subcontractor.
- **Pearlman v. Reliance Insurance Co., 371 U.S. 132:** Distinguished for its surety/property relationship; it does not establish Blue Fox's entitlement or consent here.
- **United States v. Munsey Trust Co., 332 U.S. 234:** Preserved in its governmental/surety setting; it creates no general right for an unpaid subcontractor to attach Army funds free of immunity.
sections.Law After Decision: Courts must identify the claimant's actual entitlement and the operation of the requested remedy before treating a monetary demand as specific relief under §702. A private-debt substitute does not become authorized merely through an equitable lien, a named project account, notice or the Government's failure to obtain a required bond. A genuine identified-property claim, enacted payment mandate, properly founded Tucker Act claim, recovery against an actual Miller Act surety or another unequivocal waiver remains governed by its own requirements. None is awarded here.
sections.Separate Writings: No separate writings.
sections.Procedure After Action: The case returns for dismissal of the Army lien claim for want of an applicable waiver. The rejected SBA branch remains undisturbed. No fund is reconstructed and no alternative claim or surety is created by the remand.
sections.Source Notes: The [filed petition, appendix and merits record](https://archive.org/details/micro_IA40385014_0172) establish the lower judgment, absence of bonds, notices, separate payment amounts and Blue Fox's contract-fund and post-disbursement theories. The [governing APA §702](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-1994-title5/pdf/USCODE-1994-title5-partI-chap7-sec702.pdf) supplies the waiver and its saving clauses. The asserted attachment at notice is a legal contention; it is not a finding that the Army retains property owned by Blue Fox.

header: **Case and dockets:** Humana Inc. v. Forsyth; No. 97-303; OT1998.

sections.Event:
**Humana Inc. v. Forsyth, No. 97-303.** Argued November 30, 1998; decided January 20, 1999. On writ of certiorari to the Ninth Circuit, 114 F.3d 1467. The question is whether the McCarran-Ferguson Act bars the Co-Payors' surviving federal RICO action concerning insurer fraud also prohibited by Nevada insurance law.

The Co-Payors allege concealed hospital discounts and charges of 20 percent of undiscounted bills despite a represented 80/20 allocation, during 1985–1988. The Court of Appeals permitted their overpayment claim while retaining rejection of the Premium Payors' separate RICO branch and limiting injury to overpayments actually proved. Those distinct limitations remain outside this review.
sections.Participation: All nine Justices participated at argument and decision.
sections.Public Action: The Ninth Circuit's judgment is affirmed on the McCarran-Ferguson question insofar as it permits the surviving Co-Payor RICO overpayment claim to proceed.
sections.Judgment & Remedy:
**Affirmed, 9–0, on the reviewed question.**

**Supporting:** Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer.

The Co-Payor action may proceed subject to proof of every RICO element, causation, injury and authorized remedy, with ordinary defenses intact. The Premium Payor branch is not revived. The actual-overpayment injury limit remains; a lawful statutory multiplier is a separate remedial matter. The related conspiracy-amendment instruction follows the surviving branch without establishing conspiracy or guaranteeing amendment success. The Court awards no liability, premium recovery or treble-damages amount and directs no automatic new trial.
sections.Opinion Topology:
| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to judgment | Scope joined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court | Ginsburg | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Breyer | Affirms the surviving Co-Payor branch on the reviewed question | Complete impairment rule, bounded Nevada application and all temporal, claim and remedial limits. |

All nine join; no separate writing is filed.
sections.Holdings:
#### Compatible federal fraud remedies do not impair the actual state insurance scheme

**Operative rule.** A generally applicable federal law impairs protected state insurance law when its operation contradicts the state law or frustrates an actual state policy or the administration of the state scheme; literal contradiction is not the only possible impairment. An additional private action or greater federal remedy does not itself establish impairment, and the Co-Payors' RICO claim may proceed because it targets fraud Nevada forbids while leaving the State's scheme intact and displacing no demonstrated exclusive remedial arrangement.

**Authority.** Ginsburg's Opinion of the Court has all nine Justices' direct joins and controls the rule, application and reservations.

**Controlling explanation.** The parties do not dispute here that Nevada enacted the relevant laws to regulate the business of insurance or that RICO does not specifically relate to that business. Those predicates frame the impairment question. Fabe protects policy performance and administration necessary to implement it, so the inquiry must examine the actual state policy that federal law would frustrate. Barnett Bank separately addresses an insurance-specific federal exception; RICO has no such subject matter and receives no exemption by that analogy.

The insurers correctly observe that enforcement machinery and remedial choices can form part of protected state policy. A common prohibition of fraud therefore does not by itself establish compatibility. Here, however, Nevada prohibits the alleged deception, and its regulatory authority and remedies are not established as an exclusive arrangement displaced by this Co-Payor action. RICO neither invalidates the state command nor replaces its regulator or defeats an identified policy forbidding this action or remedy. Larger federal damages alone do not establish the missing interference.

The allegations span 1985–1988. The 1987 addition of an express private remedy in Nevada Revised Statutes §686A.310 is not applied retrospectively, and the Court does not decide whether an earlier statutory action was implied. Even assuming no statutory private remedy for earlier conduct, that absence does not itself establish a policy making administrative sanctions exclusive or excluding independent federal relief. The result rests on the actual nonexclusive arrangement, not invented earlier private rights or a comprehensive state-remedy inventory.

A federal claim requiring conduct the State forbids, nullifying a state-approved practice or displacing an exclusive remedial structure established by enacted law would present impairment. No such operation, conflicting allocation of a finite insolvency estate or displacement of an administrative judgment is established here. The Court decides neither hypothetical exclusive schemes nor unrelated insurance conduct, criminal RICO or other federal laws. ERISA, antitrust, the rejected Premium Payor branch and ordinary RICO prerequisites remain unadjudicated in this review.
sections.Precedent Treatment:
- **United States Department of Treasury v. Fabe:** Applied to preserve actual state policy-performance rules and necessary administration against conflicting nonspecific federal law. It does not insulate every insurer-related act or remedy from federal law.
- **Barnett Bank of Marion County, N.A. v. Nelson:** Preserved. Its insurance-specific federal exception remains separate from the interference question and does not extend to RICO by analogy; the actual relationship between the statutes must still be examined.
sections.Law After Decision: The McCarran-Ferguson inquiry compares the operation of the federal claim with the State's actual protected policy and administration. Neither overlap nor greater federal recovery alone bars the federal claim; actual conflict or frustration can do so even without a literal contradiction. On the relationship established here, the surviving Co-Payor RICO claim complements Nevada's fraud prohibition without displacing an exclusive state mechanism. No retrospective Nevada cause of action or broader RICO entitlement is created.
sections.Separate Writings: No separate writings.
sections.Procedure After Action: The case returns to the remaining proceedings contemplated by the Ninth Circuit's judgment, with the Co-Payor claim and related amendment instruction subject to ordinary RICO requirements and defenses. Rejected Premium Payor claims and the proved-overpayment injury limitation remain unchanged. Further liability and any authorized remedy require ordinary adjudication.
sections.Source Notes: The [filed petition, appendix and merits briefs](https://archive.org/details/micro_IA40385014_0116) supply the surviving classes and claims, alleged conduct dates, remedy limitation and dispute over Nevada's pre-1987 statutory private remedy. The governing federal provision is [15 U.S.C. §1012(b)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-1994-title15/pdf/USCODE-1994-title15-chap20-sec1012.pdf); its insurance-specific exception and separate antitrust proviso retain distinct functions. The exact availability of a pre-1987 implied Nevada statutory action is unnecessary to this disposition and remains unresolved.

header: **Case and dockets:** Lopez v. Monterey County; No. 97-1396; Northern District of California No. C-91-20559-RMW.

sections.Event: Lopez v. Monterey County, No. 97-1396. Argued November 2, 1998; decided January 20, 1999. On direct review of the three-judge Northern District of California's December 19, 1997 dismissal after the Court's November 6, 1996 mandate. The questions concern the County's administration of state-mandated judicial-election changes, the reach of the 1983 submission, prospective nonuse and the dependent judicial-tenure order. California defends dismissal; the County supports the appellants.
sections.Participation: All nine Justices participated at argument and decision.
sections.Public Action: The dismissal is reversed and the case remanded; the dependent tenure-order disposition is set aside to the extent stated below.
sections.Judgment & Remedy:
**Reversed and remanded, 9–0**, with the dependent tenure-order disposition set aside insofar as based on the rejected exemption, also **9–0**.

**Supporting:** Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer.

The judgment of dismissal is reversed and the case remanded to implement the November 6, 1996 mandate. The dependent disposition of the judicial-term-extension order is set aside insofar as based on the rejected exemption. The District Court must identify the actual reach of the 1983 submission, prevent prospective use of the remaining unprecleared operative changes and apply the confined judicial-remedy rule. No officeholder outcome, completed-election consequence, damages award, new deadline or automatic Supreme Court return is directed.
sections.Opinion Topology:
| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to judgment | Scope joined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court, Parts I, II and IV | Thomas | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg, Breyer | Supports reversal and remand | Administration, actual submission and confined nonuse/judicial-plan rule. |
| Opinion of the Court, Part III | Thomas | Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg, Breyer; Stone-Zsela only as stated | Rejects the additional defenses | Eight full joins. Stone-Zsela joins rejection of delay as authorization for prospective use and of the internal-administration characterization; he agrees in rejection of the collateral-designation defense without adding grounds. |
| Opinion of the Court, Part V | Thomas | Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg, Breyer | Sets aside the dependent tenure disposition to the stated extent | Eight rationale joins; Stone-Zsela agrees in that disposition without adding grounds. |

No separate writing is filed. The Chief's disposition-only agreement on the collateral-designation defense and dependent tenure component does not supply an additional rationale.
sections.Holdings:
**Authority and scope.** Thomas delivers the opinion of the Court. The eight Associate Justices join Parts I–V. Stone-Zsela joins Parts I, II and IV, and Part III only insofar as it rejects delay as authorization for prospective use and rejects the internal-administration characterization of a direct electorate change. He agrees in rejection of the collateral-designation defense and in the dependent tenure-order disposition without adding grounds to those parts. Each controlling part thus has at least eight direct joins. No separate constitutional justification for Section 5 is adopted.

### I. State compulsion does not exempt covered administration

**Holding and operative rule.** A covered political subdivision must obtain Section 5 preclearance before administering a postbaseline voting change within that subdivision, even when a noncovered State mandates the change and leaves no local discretion. The duty attaches to the County's administration; it does not require California to submit its laws in the abstract.

**Controlling explanation.** The Court applies its November 6, 1996 Lopez mandate. That decision expressly assumed complete state displacement of local discretion and nevertheless held that giving the change operative effect is administration. The lower court's renewed reliance on state compulsion cannot reopen the settled question. Neither the 1979 law nor the January 1995 elimination of justice courts supplies an exemption from the County's duty.

Young preserves the difference between the source of a policy and its actual administration, while reserving a different question about wholly federally compelled conduct. Foreman likewise rejects the proposition that an earlier authorization automatically clears subsequent local implementation. California's argument that the County cannot choose a different arrangement confuses authority to enact with authority to administer an unprecleared change. Practical difficulty affects lawful implementation, not whether the completed mandate governs. The Court decides no discriminatory purpose, retrogressive effect or entitlement to substantive preclearance.

### II. The actual submission controls the reach of approval

**Holding and operative rule.** Replacing district electorates with a countywide electorate for judges is a covered change in voting, and a submission does not preclear earlier operative changes it failed to identify. The District Court must determine the actual reach of the 1983 submission as to the final ordinance; its attachment and the Attorney General's nonobjection do not establish blanket approval of the preceding consolidations.

**Controlling explanation.** The prior Lopez decision fixes the direct electoral character of the change and the treatment of the earlier unidentified ordinances. Presley distinguishes internal allocation of governmental authority from changes in who votes for an official; this alteration concerns the electorate itself. Allen and Perkins preserve coverage of such practical electoral changes.

McCain and Clark require identification of what was submitted. Young and Foreman preserve that submission-specific boundary. The 1983 additional-judgeships submission, attached final ordinance and nonobjection are relevant evidence, but they do not establish the operative terms needed to decide conclusively whether the final ordinance itself was approved. That question remains for determination below. The Court does not invalidate an actual approval, review the merits of the Attorney General's decision, or treat an unavailable source as a party's failure to comply.

### III. Delay and a collateral designation challenge do not authorize prospective use

**Holding and operative rule.** Delay does not authorize prospective administration of an operative covered change that lacks preclearance, and the effective Section 4(b) coverage determination cannot be collaterally retried in this Section 5 enforcement action. Statutory bailout remains a distinct route; reliance, completed acts and practical timing may bear on legally available retrospective relief or a lawful transition, without supplying clearance.

**Controlling explanation.** California's remaining defenses must be separated rather than treated as another version of compulsion. Lopez already resolved prospective nonuse and the improper collateral challenge to designation. Clark and Hampton County preserve attention to remedial circumstances without making delay an authorization to use an uncleared practice. The direct change in judicial electorates likewise cannot be recast as merely internal administration under Presley. These applications enforce the existing mandate; they announce no new facial constitutional holding, decide no bailout request and create no general retrospective equitable rule.

### IV. Nonuse and the confined judicial-plan alternative

**Holding and operative rule.** The District Court must prevent prospective use of established operative changes lacking preclearance until approval is obtained through the Attorney General or the District Court for the District of Columbia. A necessary temporary plan wholly formulated by the federal court is distinct only if supported by independent lawful remedial authority, consistent with the Constitution and Voting Rights Act, no more displacing of state law than necessity requires, and limited to the period before a lawful precleared arrangement becomes available.

**Controlling explanation.** Connor distinguishes a genuinely judicial plan from governmental policy, and McDaniel prevents a governmental plan from becoming exempt merely through judicial adoption. Lopez and Young apply that distinction while preserving nonuse. The lawful alternatives include the lawful precleared baseline, completed preclearance, or an independently justified judicial plan meeting the stated limits. The Court selects none here and does not authorize a court to adopt the County's policy as its own.

Clark left open whether extreme circumstances could justify allowing an election to proceed while preclearance remained pending. No such circumstance is established here, and ordinary administrative difficulty supplies no exception. The earlier ordinary six-year at-large elections did not qualify under the prior mandate. Shaw preserves substantive purpose-and-effect determinations for the designated preclearance forums. The enforcement court's task is coverage, actual submission and lawful implementation, not its own substantive approval.

### V. The dependent tenure order requires lawful reconsideration

**Holding and operative rule.** The disposition of the judicial-term-extension order must be set aside insofar as it depends on the rejected exemption and reconsidered under the corrected legal premise and actual circumstances. Reversal does not automatically revive an expired arrangement, extend any judge's tenure, install or remove an officeholder, cancel a completed election or invalidate judicial acts.

**Controlling explanation.** The District Court vacated its September 25, 1996 extension order together with dismissal of the enforcement action. Once the exemption premise fails, that dependent disposition cannot stand on the same ground. Its correction nevertheless requires lawful authority and the actual tenure circumstances; the mandate did not select officeholders or create indefinite holdovers.

Prior preclearance of a four-division option resolves only its preclearance status. It does not settle independent state-law, electorate-and-jurisdiction linkage, population, divided-municipality, residence or remedial-authority questions. Johnson's rejection of a design-only racial injury likewise does not approve all features of a proposed arrangement. The District Court must apply the existing mandate to the actual remaining questions without treating preclearance as complete legal approval. No new submission deadline, compulsory hearing or automatic return to this Court is ordered.
sections.Precedent Treatment:
- **Lopez v. Monterey County, November 6, 1996:** Enforced unchanged as the governing administration, direct-electorate, submission, nonuse and confined-remedy mandate; its state-compulsion question is not reopened.
- **Young v. Fordice, March 31, 1997:** Applied for actual administration, identified submission and the limits on judicial implementation; its wholly federal-compulsion reservation remains distinct.
- **Foreman v. Dallas County, June 27, 1997:** Applied to preserve actual baselines and submission-specific approval; authorization does not automatically approve later implementation.
- **Presley v. Etowah County Commission:** Distinguished because the electorate changes directly; its internal-governance boundary remains.
- **Allen v. State Board of Elections:** Applied to direct changes affecting electoral choice, without deciding discriminatory purpose or effect.
- **Perkins v. Matthews:** Applied to practical electoral operation rather than the label or source of the change.
- **McCain v. Lybrand:** Applied to require identification of the submitted change; related material does not establish blanket approval.
- **Clark v. Roemer:** Applied for specific submission and prospective nonuse; its reserved extreme-circumstance possibility is not established here.
- **NAACP v. Hampton County Election Commission:** Applied to distinguish prospective compliance from properly bounded remedial attention to actual circumstances.
- **Connor v. Johnson:** Preserved for a necessary plan wholly formulated by the court within independent lawful authority.
- **McDaniel v. Sanchez:** Applied to distinguish judicial adoption of governmental policy from a wholly judicial plan.
- **Shaw v. Reno:** Applied at the entering law's stated boundary preserving designated substantive-preclearance channels, without a new constitutional merits ruling.
- **Johnson v. Miller:** Its rule against a design-only racial injury remains distinct from other constitutional, state-law and remedial objections to a proposed judicial-election plan.
sections.Law After Decision: The County's obligation to preclear administered changes is unchanged. State compulsion, delay and attachment of a related ordinance do not dispense with it. The actual scope of the 1983 approval remains to be determined. Prospective nonuse must be enforced, with any genuinely judicial temporary plan meeting every stated necessity, authority, legal-compliance and duration limit. The dependent tenure question returns for lawful reconsideration without automatic reinstatement or a selected replacement system.
sections.Separate Writings: None. The Chief joins Parts I, II and IV and the stated prospective-nonuse and electorate propositions of Part III. He agrees in rejection of the collateral-designation defense and the dependent-tenure disposition without adding grounds.
sections.Procedure After Action: The judgment of dismissal is reversed and the case remanded to implement the November 6, 1996 mandate. The dependent disposition of the judicial-term-extension order is set aside insofar as based on the rejected exemption. The District Court must identify the actual reach of the 1983 submission, prevent prospective use of the remaining unprecleared operative changes and apply the confined judicial-remedy rule. No officeholder outcome, completed-election consequence, damages award, new deadline or automatic Supreme Court return is directed.
sections.Source Notes: The [published record and procedural recitations, 525 U.S. 266](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-525/pdf/USREPORTS-525-266.pdf), support the dates, later dismissal, 1983 submission history and dependent extension-order issue. The actual operative submission terms and current tenure circumstances are not established sufficiently here to command blanket approval or a specific officeholder result; those questions remain for lawful determination below. Source limits do not establish a failure by a litigant to make a required filing.

header: **Case and dockets:** Citizens for a Constitutional Convention v. Yoshina; No. 98-671; Ninth Circuit Nos. 97-16408, 97-16543, 97-16540 and 97-16596.

sections.Event:
*Citizens for a Constitutional Convention v. Yoshina*, No. 98-671. Merits decision, January 21, 1999, October Term 1998. On writ of certiorari to the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit; *Bennett v. Yoshina*, 140 F.3d 1218, decided March 27, 1998, amended June 23, 1998. No separate Supreme Court argument date is established.

The question is whether Hawaii's post-election construction counting blanks in the approval denominator violated due process or the First Amendment, and whether the November 1998 referendum ended the controversy. In 1996 the question received 163,869 yes votes, 160,153 no votes, 45,245 blanks and 90 overvotes. The Hawaii Supreme Court construed Article XVII, §2 to include submitted blanks in the denominator and distinguished the language governing amendment ratification. The district court ordered a new referendum; plaintiffs sought certification that the 1996 proposal passed. The Ninth Circuit rejected the federal claims, vacated the new-election injunction and its stay, and dismissed the dependent cross-appeal and intervention appeals in light of that merits resolution.

Act 131 placed another convention question on the November 1998 ballot. It received 140,688 yes votes, 244,753 no votes, 26,784 blanks and 295 overvotes and failed under either denominator. Petitioners nonetheless maintained their demand to recognize asserted 1996 approval. The later vote is therefore addressed as a change in remedial circumstances, not as a decision of the earlier federal claim.
sections.Participation: Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer participate.
sections.Public Action: The judgment of the Ninth Circuit is affirmed.
sections.Judgment & Remedy:
**Affirmed, 9–0.**

**Supporting:** Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer.

The rejection of both federal constitutional claims and the vacatur of the district court's new-election injunction and associated stay stand. Certification of 1996 approval is denied because the asserted federal violation is not established. No third referendum is ordered. The Court does not vacate the merits judgment for mootness, award a new fee amount, or independently decide intervention entitlement. Any still-pending collateral matter retains its actual procedural posture.
sections.Opinion Topology:
| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to judgment | Scope joined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court | Souter | Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer in full; Stone-Zsela in Parts I and II and the remedial disposition | Supports affirmance | Parts I and II: live controversy, federal review and due process; Part III: First Amendment; disposition: affirmance and denial of the requested constitutional relief |

Stone-Zsela concurs in the judgment rejecting the First Amendment claim, without joining Part III or adding a ground. No separate opinion is filed.
sections.Holdings:
### I. A live federal claim survives the second referendum

**Holding and operative rule:** A later referendum does not moot a substantial federal claim seeking recognition of an asserted entitlement created by the earlier vote when that relief remains capable of addressing a continuing injury. These plaintiffs maintain that claim; their ultimate failure to establish it does not eliminate jurisdiction.

**Authority:** Souter's opinion, joined by all eight other Justices, controls this threshold holding and Part II. Part III has the different coalition stated there.

**Controlling explanation:** The Court holds that the November 1998 vote does not dispose of the maintained demand to give legal effect to the asserted 1996 approval. Act 131 submitted a new question without expressly extinguishing that asserted entitlement. *Church of Scientology* separates the possibility of meaningful relief from ultimate entitlement to it; *Spencer* requires an actual surviving interest, which the maintained certification demand supplies here. *Steel Co.*, *NAACP v. Jones* and *Wisconsin Right to Life v. Paradise* require jurisdiction before contested merits and distinguish a substantial but unsuccessful claim from an absent controversy. Fees alone, hypothetical damages and an unproved collateral ruling supply no jurisdictional premise.

The federal plaintiffs were not parties to the state action, and the two organizations' participation as friends of the court did not make them parties. The bar against lower federal appellate review of a state-court loser's judgment therefore does not foreclose their own federal claim. The authoritative state construction remains binding as state law. Under *Ex parte Young*, a claim for future implementation of a federal right against responsible officials is not a demand for retrospective damages; under *Pennhurst*, it cannot become an instruction to follow a different federal construction of state law. This permits consideration of the constitutional claim without deciding the precise certification order available had a violation been proved. No mootness-based vacatur follows.

### II. The record does not establish fundamental unfairness

**Holding and operative rule:** A state court's neutral interpretation of an ambiguous election provision does not violate due process merely because election officials earlier gave a contrary advisory interpretation. Federal relief remains available for fundamentally unfair administration, but the dissemination, reliance and voting circumstances here do not establish the pervasive deprivation needed to overturn the 1996 legal result or certify approval.

**Authority:** Part II of Souter's opinion is joined by all eight other Justices; it states the Court's controlling due-process rule and application.

**Controlling explanation:** The Court holds that official misinformation and authoritative construction of state law require distinct examination. A legally possible construction does not by itself answer a claim of actual official inducement, and informal guidance is not irrelevant merely because it lacked power to amend the Constitution. The polling-place sheet explained yes and no choices but said nothing about blanks. The contrary fact sheet had limited distribution. Statements to proponents and allegations of individual reliance matter, but campaigning reliance and a voter's inability to cast an effective choice are different injuries. Every submitted ballot was counted; voters had ready yes and no choices; and the record does not establish the election-wide frustration asserted.

*Burdick* requires consideration of the actual burden and the State's precise interests. Requiring affirmative support among those submitting ballots serves Hawaii's legitimate decision whether to convene a constitution-making body. Its highest court's distinction between convention and amendment-ratification language is not facially arbitrary. *Griffin v. Burns* and *Roe v. Alabama*, persuasive lower-court decisions, concern materially different changes affecting ballots cast through or withheld from officially described absentee procedures; neither makes every administrative mistake a federal violation. *Smiley* preserves the difference between interpretive authority and displacement of settled guidance; it supplies no universal immunity for retrospective change.

The Court does not find that no individual relied, that every abstainer was indifferent, or that deliberate misleading directions can never justify relief. It rejects the constitutional premise for the relief sought on this record without recounting the election under a different rule of state law.

### III. A denominator rule does not compel political speech

**Holding and operative rule:** A neutral referendum-approval threshold may include blank ballots in the denominator without compelling voters to espouse opposition when blanks remain accurately counted and reported as blanks and the rule does not discriminate among identifiable voters. The legal consequence of abstention does not itself supply the asserted First Amendment violation.

**Authority:** Part III of Souter's opinion is joined by Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer. Those eight Justices supply a controlling majority. Stone-Zsela agrees only with rejection of this claim and adds no ground.

**Controlling explanation:** The Court holds that determining how much affirmative support a convention requires differs from attributing a political message to an unwilling voter. *Gordon v. Lance* permits nondiscriminatory heightened approval requirements; *Burdick* rejects a general entitlement to use the official ballot as an expressive tally. Here the State did not relabel blanks as affirmative no votes, alter recorded yes or no choices, require a public statement, or suppress advocacy outside the ballot. *Buckley v. American Constitutional Law Foundation* concerns an actual requirement of personal identification during political solicitation and therefore does not govern this denominator rule. The claim that abstention makes approval harder does not establish compelled speech. The Court grants no general permission falsely to attribute political views to nonconsenting voters.
sections.Precedent Treatment:
- *Church of Scientology of California v. United States* is applied to distinguish possible meaningful relief from success on the merits; it retains that distinction.
- *Spencer v. Kemna* is applied to require a concrete continuing interest; the maintained 1996 recognition claim supplies it here.
- *Steel Co. v. Citizens for a Better Environment*, *NAACP, Los Angeles Branch v. Jones* and *Wisconsin Right to Life v. Paradise* are applied to keep Article III injury and substantial merits failure separate; none permits jurisdiction to be assumed.
- *Rooker v. Fidelity Trust Co.* and *District of Columbia Court of Appeals v. Feldman* are distinguished because these federal claimants were not losing parties in the state action; the Court does not reopen state-law construction.
- *Ex parte Young* is applied to the prospective federal claim against officials; *Pennhurst State School & Hospital v. Halderman* retains its bar against directing state officials on a federal court's contrary view of state law.
- *Burdick v. Takushi* is applied to actual burdens and justified administration and to the absence of a general expressive-ballot entitlement. Its contextual inquiry remains intact.
- *Smiley v. Citibank* is distinguished from an automatic answer to an election-reliance claim; its reservation concerning displacement of settled guidance remains.
- *Gordon v. Lance* is applied to nondiscriminatory heightened approval requirements; no new discriminatory threshold is approved.
- *Buckley v. American Constitutional Law Foundation* is distinguished because its personal-attribution burden is absent here.
- *U.S. Bancorp Mortgage Co. v. Bonner Mall Partnership* remains undisturbed: the equitable vacatur question premised on subsequent mootness does not arise for this continuing merits controversy.
sections.Law After Decision: As of January 21, 1999, this record supplies no federal right to certify the 1996 convention proposal as approved or require another vote. Due process still reaches fundamentally unfair election administration; lawful state interpretive authority alone does not immunize materially different official inducement. The First Amendment distinguishes neutral approval thresholds from compelled attribution. A subsequent election does not automatically extinguish a concrete maintained claim to the legal effect of an earlier vote. No state constitutional counting rule is rewritten, and no broader rule concerning deliberately misleading directions is established.
sections.Separate Writings: No separate opinion is filed. Stone-Zsela agrees in the judgment rejecting the independent First Amendment claim without adding a ground or joining Part III.
sections.Procedure After Action: The Ninth Circuit's rejection of federal relief remains effective, including its direction for judgment for the officials and vacatur of the new-election injunction and stay. The dependent proceedings yield no separate entitlement to certification or a fresh election. No additional merits remand or scheduled Supreme Court act is required. Collateral motions, if still pending, remain for disposition under their actual posture and ordinary law; no unverified post-December ruling or fee award is entered.
sections.Source Notes: The amended *Bennett v. Yoshina*, 140 F.3d 1218, opinion supplies the federal posture, information sheets, alleged reliance and ballot treatment. *Hawaii State AFL-CIO v. Yoshina*, 84 Haw. 374, 935 P.2d 89, supplies the authoritative state construction. Act 131, approved June 22, 1998, and the [official November 1998 Hawaii report](https://files.hawaii.gov/elections/files/results/1998/general/histatewide.pdf) establish the later election. Petitioners' December 3 supplement and December 24 reply maintain certification-related relief; the State's opposition contests its availability. The record does not establish a later disposition of the reported collateral motions. No exact Supreme Court oral-argument date is supplied. The judicial propositions above are paraphrases, not attributed quotations.

header: **Case and dockets:** AT&T Corp. v. Iowa Utilities Board; Nos. 97-826, 97-829, 97-830, 97-831, 97-1075, 97-1087, 97-1099 and 97-1141; including California respondents in the AT&T, MCI and FCC petitions.

sections.Event:
*AT&T Corp. v. Iowa Utilities Board* and consolidated cases, Nos. 97-826, 97-829, 97-830, 97-831, 97-1075, 97-1087, 97-1099 and 97-1141. Argued October 13, 1998; decided January 25, 1999, October Term 1998. On writs of certiorari to the Eighth Circuit; *Iowa Utilities Board v. FCC*, 120 F.3d 753, with its amended rehearing decision, and *California v. FCC*, 124 F.3d 934.

The Telecommunications Act of 1996 imposed interconnection, resale and unbundled-access duties to open local telephone markets. The FCC's First Report and Order implemented those duties through national rules addressing pricing methodology, state proceedings and required elements. The Eighth Circuit rejected federal authority over several subjects, vacated rules on that and other grounds, and sustained other portions. Its October 1997 amended combination ruling vacated Rule 51.315(b)–(f), adding existing combinations to its earlier affirmative-combination decision. The separate California judgment vacated intraLATA toll-dialing-parity rules on the authority ground and treated the numbering-cost challenge as unripe.

The questions concern national implementing authority, the actual statutory access criteria, the network-element definition and ownership prerequisite, existing and new combinations, superior quality, individual agreement arrangements and the separate threshold questions. AT&T expressly sought reconsideration of the feasibility presumption, superior-quality duties and affirmative combinations under the correct authority standard. The two judgments and eight dockets remain one consolidated matter with distinct component mandates.
sections.Participation: Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer participate at argument and decision.
sections.Public Action: The two judgments are affirmed in part, reversed in part and vacated in part, and the cases are remanded for the component dispositions stated below.
