sections.Judgment & Remedy: The conforming implementing decree is entered. It establishes the described boundary, enjoins New York from enforcing its laws or asserting sovereignty over territory assigned to New Jersey within the decree's defined scope, retains implementing jurisdiction, and divides the Special Master's compensation, assistance and litigation expenses equally. No numerical tally or individual lineup is announced.
sections.Opinion Topology: Unsigned decree of the Court. No signed opinion or new noted adherence statement accompanies it.
sections.Holdings:
#### Geographic implementation of the existing judgment

**Operative rule:** The six-part instrument and incorporated map fix the interstate boundary under the prior judgment: New Jersey retains the later artificial fill, and New York retains the original island to its 1834 low-water line, including the accepted historical filled pier once. The complete perimeter controls; neither approximate acreage nor a separately added pier parcel replaces it.

**Authority:** The Court's implementing decree gives effect to the May 26, 1998 judgment. It discloses no individual vote or lineup.

**Controlling explanation:** The Court holds the description consistent with the entitlement already adjudicated. New Jersey v. New York supplies the Compact allocation and requires accurate implementation rather than an administratively convenient territorial exchange. One perimeter incorporates the original island and historical pier without double counting. The description and map implement that line without reopening prescription or awarding land by an acreage target. Retained jurisdiction permits proceedings needed to give the decree proper force and effect; it does not decide unrelated municipal regulation, taxation, private title, federal monument administration, public access, damages or later reclamation.
sections.Precedent Treatment: New Jersey v. New York, decided May 26, 1998, is implemented without changing its Compact construction, territorial entitlement, rejected exchange or reserved questions.
sections.Law After Decision: The adjudicated entitlement now has an entered geographic decree and enforceable implementing directions. No new constitutional rule or broader ownership, taxation or regulatory holding is announced.
sections.Procedure After Action: The decree takes effect as the Court's implementing disposition. The Court retains jurisdiction for proceedings, orders and writs needed to give it proper force and effect and effectuate the parties' rights. The States share the stated Special Master expenses equally. No return date is set.
sections.Source Notes: The complete geographic description and December 1, 1998 map appear in the [official United States Reports, volume 526, pages 589–601 and accompanying map](https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/boundvolumes/526bv.pdf). They are incorporated above; approximate acreage is not an independent territorial award.

header: **Case and dockets:** Ruhrgas AG v. Marathon Oil Co.; No. 98-470; judgment below, 145 F.3d 211.

sections.Event: Ruhrgas AG v. Marathon Oil Co., No. 98-470. Merits decision, May 17, 1999; argued March 22, 1999. On certiorari to the Fifth Circuit, 145 F.3d 211. In a removed Texas action concerning a Norwegian gas venture, the District Court dismissed for lack of personal jurisdiction without resolving three asserted removal grounds. The en banc Court of Appeals required subject-matter jurisdiction to be addressed first. The question is whether that order is invariably required.
sections.Participation: Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer participated at argument and decision.
sections.Public Action: The Court reverses the en banc judgment and remands for further appellate proceedings.
sections.Judgment & Remedy: Reversed and remanded, 9–0. Supporting: Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer. The District Court was permitted to choose the personal-jurisdiction inquiry. The Fifth Circuit must review the dismissal under the correct sequencing rule; the Court does not affirm the correctness of the disputed contacts or the ultimate personal-jurisdiction conclusion. No removal ground or state-court remand is decided.

sections.Holdings:
#### A court may choose a straightforward nonmerits jurisdictional ground

**Holding and operative rule:** A federal court may dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction before resolving subject-matter jurisdiction when personal jurisdiction is straightforward and presents no complex state-law question while the subject-matter issue is difficult. Ordinarily an easily resolved subject-matter question should come first; the choice must respect applicable statutory remand commands and review bars and must decide no contested merits.

**Authority:** Scalia's opinion, joined by all nine Justices, controls the rule, application and remedy.

**Controlling explanation:** The Court holds that declining authority over a defendant does not assume authority to decide liability. Citizens for a Better Environment v. Steel Co. forbids assumed Article III power for contested merits, and NAACP, Los Angeles Branch v. Jones applies that boundary to constitutional claims. Neither exhausts the order among nonmerits thresholds. Personal jurisdiction protects a defendant's interest in being subject to the court's authority; its waivability does not make it an optional prerequisite to a binding merits judgment. Here choosing that straightforward ground avoids an unnecessary difficult subject-matter determination without deciding the tort claims. The State's forum interest and the possible consequences of jurisdictional determinations remain relevant to the choice, but do not establish an absolute order. If subject matter is as readily resolved and personal jurisdiction raises difficult state law, comity ordinarily favors deciding remand first. Murphy Brothers keeps removal timing distinct from actual jurisdiction, and El Paso Natural Gas gives effect to a particular statutory priority rather than a universal hierarchy. An established absence of subject-matter jurisdiction retains its statutory consequence; an unresolved difficult issue is not the same thing. The Court leaves the correctness of the actual personal-jurisdiction dismissal to the Court of Appeals and decides none of the three asserted removal grounds.
sections.Precedent Treatment:
- Citizens for a Better Environment v. Steel Co. is applied within its express scope: jurisdiction must precede contested merits, but its nonmerits-sequencing reservation permits today's rule.
- NAACP, Los Angeles Branch v. Jones is applied on the same merits boundary; its prohibition on assumed standing is unchanged.
- Murphy Brothers, Inc. v. Michetti Pipe Stringing, Inc. is distinguished as removal timing and formal process, which establish no subject-matter jurisdiction or universal sequence.
- El Paso Natural Gas Co. v. Neztsosie is distinguished as a statute-specific priority over prudential exhaustion, not a general order between jurisdictional grounds.
- Insurance Corp. of Ireland v. Compagnie des Bauxites de Guinee supplies the distinction between the individual interest protected by personal jurisdiction and institutional subject-matter limits; the distinction does not establish an invariable order.
sections.Law After Decision: Federal courts may use the bounded personal-jurisdiction-first route in removed as well as originally filed actions. The rule adds discretion among nonmerits thresholds while preserving ordinary comity, actual statutory commands and the prohibition on deciding contested merits without jurisdiction. It establishes no universal preclusion rule or actual jurisdiction over these claims.
sections.Procedure After Action: The case returns to the Fifth Circuit for further proceedings, including review of the personal-jurisdiction dismissal under the permitted sequence. No merits determination, state-court remand, new discovery or later Supreme Court event is commanded.
sections.Source Notes: The lower-court chronology and distinct removal theories appear in the [official United States Reports, volume 526, pages 574–588](https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/boundvolumes/526bv.pdf) and the en banc judgment at 145 F.3d 211. Review is confined to sequencing; the correctness of the personal-jurisdiction dismissal remains outside the question decided.

header: **Case and dockets:** Saenz v. Roe; No. 98-97; judgment below, Roe v. Anderson, 134 F.3d 1400.

sections.Event: Saenz v. Roe, No. 98-97. Argued January 13, 1999; decided May 17, 1999. On writ of certiorari to the Ninth Circuit, which affirmed a single judge's preliminary injunction in Roe v. Anderson, 134 F.3d 1400. The question is whether California may limit otherwise eligible bona fide residents during their first year to the benefits available in their former State, and whether federal statutory permission sustains that classification.
sections.Participation: Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer participated in the consideration and decision.
sections.Public Action: The judgment affirming the preliminary injunction is affirmed.
sections.Judgment & Remedy:
**Affirmed, 8–1.**

**Supporting:** Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer.

**Opposing:** Thomas.

The preliminary injunction remains in effect against the first-year differential. No permanent decree, damages award or fixed benefit amount is entered.
sections.Opinion Topology: Justice Kennedy delivers the Opinion of the Court, joined in full by Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer. Justice Thomas dissents. All eight majority Justices directly join both holdings and the bounded remedy.
sections.Holdings:
### Bona fide new citizens receive equal ordinary welfare treatment

**Holding and operative rule:** A United States citizen who establishes bona fide residence in a State becomes its citizen on equal terms; the Fourteenth Amendment's Citizenship and Privileges or Immunities provisions forbid lowering that otherwise eligible citizen's ordinary welfare benefits solely because of recent arrival or the former State's benefit amount. California's first-year differential violates that guarantee even if the person never received benefits before moving or moved for reasons unrelated to assistance.

**Authority:** Kennedy's Opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer, controls both holdings, eight votes.

**Controlling explanation:** The Court compares current citizens within their present State. Slaughter-House specifically recognizes a citizen's ability to settle in another State and become its citizen; the Court applies that limited proposition without reopening the decision's whole account of the Clause. Shapiro rejects durational welfare penalties, Dunn distinguishes genuine residence from added duration, and Zobel rejects allocation of ordinary resident benefits by arrival history. The State cannot answer that inequality by observing that a newcomer receives no less than in the former State. Prior benefits do not define present citizenship, and eventual equality does not cure twelve months of inferior treatment. Saving money is a legitimate general objective, but selecting new citizens for the saving merely restates the challenged disadvantage. This is equality within a program California has chosen, not a constitutional entitlement to a program or a national benefit level. Bona fide residence verification and genuinely equal prospective eligibility rules remain available. The decision does not govern distinct services or contributions earned elsewhere or supply a general catalogue of privileges. The implementing instructions' exclusion of families newly arriving from another country does not cure the discrimination among current citizens who moved from another State.

### Federal permission cannot lower the constitutional floor

**Holding and operative rule:** Congress may structure and condition federal welfare assistance, but may not authorize a State to violate the Fourteenth Amendment's equal-citizenship guarantee. Section 604(c)'s permission to use prior-State benefit levels therefore cannot sustain California's unconstitutional differential; permission is not a federal command.

**Controlling explanation:** Boerne distinguishes enforcement of a constitutional guarantee from replacement of its content. The federal provision does not change the fact that California administers unequal treatment among bona fide current citizens. Statutory permission cannot remove the protection that makes the classification invalid. The Court does not invalidate every federal welfare provision, require a nationwide program design or decide a constitutionally distinct nationwide rule. Thomas accepts the general inability to authorize a proved violation but disputes the underlying guarantee's application; that disagreement does not make the permission defense sufficient once this classification is held unconstitutional.
sections.Precedent Treatment:
- The Slaughter-House Cases supply the specific recognition of becoming another State's citizen through bona fide residence; their broader construction is not reopened.
- Shapiro v. Thompson supplies the prohibition on durational welfare penalties; a reduced payment still burdens current equality.
- Dunn v. Blumstein distinguishes actual residence from additional duration.
- Zobel v. Williams rejects ordinary resident-benefit allocation by arrival history.
- City of Boerne v. Flores prevents statutory replacement of constitutional content.
- Lunding and Romer retain their source-specific equality rules; neither is converted into a general judicial guarantee of welfare amounts.
sections.Law After Decision: California must treat otherwise eligible bona fide current citizens equally in ordinary welfare benefits without the first-year prior-State ceiling. Legitimate residence verification and equal eligibility conditions remain enforceable. The ruling rests on narrow equal state citizenship, creates no national welfare amount and cannot be displaced by federal permission. No precedent is overruled.
sections.Separate Writings: Justice Thomas would reverse. His provision-specific approach, reflected in Lunding and Boerne, requires an established constitutional basis before ordinary benefit distinctions receive heightened protection. He does not regard the historical foundation offered for Privileges or Immunities as sufficient to constitutionalize this welfare-equality rule. He distinguishes Shapiro's complete denial of essential assistance from a temporary continuation of prior-State benefits and would sustain the fiscal classification under ordinary review. He acknowledges that Congress cannot authorize an actual Fourteenth Amendment violation, but finds none here. He does not direct any unrelated residence or eligibility finding.
sections.Procedure After Action: The preliminary injunction continues, and ordinary proceedings resume consistent with the resolved constitutional rule. California may verify bona fide residence and apply lawful equal eligibility rules, but may not use recent arrival or former-State rates to impose this first-year reduction. No permanent injunction, damages, national redesign or particular payment amount is ordered by this judgment.
sections.Source Notes: The reviewed appellate judgment is Roe v. Anderson, 134 F.3d 1400. The actual preliminary posture, state classification and permissive federal provision appear in [526 U.S. 489](https://www.law.cornell.edu/supct/html/98-97.ZO.html). The state rule's prior-benefit and motive independence is preserved; no new individual eligibility finding is made.

header: **Case and dockets:** Maine Green Party v. Maine; First Circuit No. 98-1309.

sections.Event:
Maine Green Party v. Maine, First Circuit No. 98-1309. Merits decision, May 20, 1999, on review of the First Circuit's March 2, 1999 judgment, 173 F.3d 1, affirming summary judgment for Maine. The question concerns the five-percent presidential-vote condition for retaining statewide party recognition and the asserted right to organize locally. No Supreme Court argument date is established.

The party qualified through Jonathan Carter's 6.4% gubernatorial vote in 1994 and lost recognition after Ralph Nader received less than five percent in the 1996 presidential election. The initial papers challenged the condition and asserted organizational autonomy; the parties dispute whether the later exclusive-local theory introduced a materially different factual premise. An affidavit described efforts toward national organization. The First Circuit majority affirmed on preservation; Campbell concurred on the merits.
sections.Participation: All nine Justices participate: Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer.
sections.Public Action: The First Circuit's judgment is affirmed. No injunction, recognition order or further merits remand is entered.
sections.Judgment & Remedy:
**Affirmed, 5–4.**

**Supporting:** Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Scalia, Thomas and Breyer.
**Opposing:** Stevens, Kennedy, Souter and Ginsburg.

The judgment rejecting this challenge remains in force. Four affirm on preservation; the Chief concurs on the facial merits and leaves concrete as-applied exclusion claims open. The four dissenters would vacate and remand for ordinary examination, without ordering recognition, an injunction or a new election.
sections.Opinion Topology:
| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to judgment | Scope joined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Lead opinion announcing the judgment | Breyer | O'Connor, Scalia, Thomas | Supports affirmance | Procedural preservation ground only; no constitutional merits holding. |
| Opinion concurring in the judgment | Stone-Zsela | No other Justice | Supports affirmance | Preserved legal argument; facial merits on the established record, with concrete as-applied claims open. |
| Dissent | Stevens | Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg | Would vacate and remand | Preserved legal organizational-autonomy argument; ordinary factual and constitutional examination, without final merits determination. |

No opinion commands a majority rationale for affirmance. The Chief and the four dissenters directly agree on the bounded preservation proposition stated below; their distinct judgments and writings remain separate.
sections.Holdings:
### A refined legal argument does not itself forfeit the original associational claim

**Holding and operative rule:** A party that initially challenged the presidential-vote condition and asserted its right to choose its organizational structure does not lose that legal organizational-autonomy objection merely by sharpening it later. That conclusion neither proves an exclusive local philosophy nor permits new summary-judgment facts to be assumed; the national-organizing affidavit and the factual basis of the as-applied theory retain their ordinary evidentiary significance.

**Authority:** Stone-Zsela's concurrence and Stevens's dissent, joined by Kennedy, Souter and Ginsburg, directly adopt this same limited proposition. Those five votes control the legal-argument distinction, without supplying a majority rationale for the judgment or a command to reopen this case.

**Controlling explanation:** Yee permits a different legal argument supporting a properly presented federal claim while preserving distinct limits on facts and the question presented. Here the original challenge identified the same presidential-vote condition and the asserted freedom to organize as the members chose. The later legal formulation therefore is not wholly new merely because it gives that associational objection greater precision. The contrary position correctly identifies a possible difference between inability to build a national party and a philosophical refusal to do so. That difference prevents a court from assuming the asserted philosophy; it does not itself erase the originally presented legal objection. Thomas v. Arn permits reasonable, nonjurisdictional presentation rules, but its failure-to-object setting does not automatically decide an argument raised in objections. The district court's silence establishes neither a new fact nor an express waiver ruling. This conclusion makes no factual finding about exclusive-local intent and resolves no constitutional merits.

### The affirmance has no controlling constitutional rationale

**Judgment without controlling rationale:** Five Justices affirm, but the four-Justice preservation ground and the Chief's contextual merits ground are not logical subsets of one another. Marks yields no common narrower rationale. The judgment binds the parties; it establishes no general five-percent safe harbor, no duty to participate nationally, and no Court holding approving every alternative ballot route or rejecting every concrete as-applied exclusion claim.
sections.Precedent Treatment:
- Yee v. City of Escondido is applied by the five Justices supporting the preserved-legal-argument proposition; its separate factual and granted-question limits remain.
- Thomas v. Arn remains a rule allowing nonjurisdictional presentation requirements, not a mandatory forfeiture rule for every theory raised in objections.
- Marks v. United States supplies no common affirmance rationale because the procedural and merits grounds are independent.
- Anderson v. Celebrezze retains contextual review of actual burden, precise interests and fit; no majority adopts a new retention-rule application.
- Burdick v. Takushi retains its calibrated framework and complete-system limits; no new constitutional application commands five here.
- Norman v. Reed retains its actual-access and separate-electorate protections without a majority retention-rule application.
- Timmons v. Twin Cities Area New Party retains its specific nonfusion holding; no majority extends it to validate this condition.
- National Committee of the Reform Party v. Democratic National Committee retains its support-sensitive financing scope and supplies no general retention safe harbor.
- Buckley v. American Constitutional Law Foundation retains its petition-advocacy protections; no majority changes them in this case.
sections.Law After Decision: The reviewed judgment stands. The bounded legal-argument preservation proposition has five direct supporters, but the Court establishes no constitutional safe harbor for presidential-vote retention and no unconditional right to statewide party privileges based on local success. Existing contextual ballot-access scrutiny remains unchanged. Concrete as-applied exclusion claims require their own properly available proceedings and supported record; this judgment orders no new proceeding.
sections.Separate Writings:
**Breyer, joined by O'Connor, Scalia and Thomas, announcing the judgment:** These Justices would affirm because an as-applied case based on practical difficulty building a national organization differs materially from one based on an exclusive philosophical commitment to local politics. Yee protects new legal arguments, not assumed new facts. The affidavit describing national organization efforts makes the change consequential. The State's undeveloped objection and the district court's unexplained adoption do not prevent enforcement of ordinary presentation requirements. Arn supports reasonable nonjurisdictional management but does not make every omitted theory jurisdictionally barred. They reach no constitutional merits, approve no universal presidential-support proxy and find no alternative route necessarily adequate.

**Stone-Zsela, concurring in the judgment:** The initial organizational-autonomy argument and Eu and Tashjian citations preserve the legal objection, while the affidavit prevents an unsupported finding of an exclusively local philosophy. Applying Anderson–Burdick and Timmons to this record, he would reject the facial challenge because statewide administrative privileges may depend on demonstrated statewide support and workable alternative access remains available. The party can organize, endorse and campaign; its 1994 qualification through a nonparty gubernatorial candidate demonstrates an operative route. The record does not establish practically prohibitive requalification or alternative access. This is not automatic deference to the statewide label, a duty to nominate a presidential candidate, or approval of every retention and qualification rule. A developed record of compelled abandonment of genuinely local organization without a workable ballot alternative would require a different burden-and-fit inquiry.

The routes remain distinct: section 301 governs retention, with caucus, convention and certification conditions; section 302 permits formation through a consenting qualifying nonparty candidate, together with enrollment, caucuses in all sixteen counties and a convention; section 303 provides petition qualification. Its approved form, verified and certified signatures and legal addresses equal to five percent of the last gubernatorial vote, and filing before 5 p.m. on the 180th day before a primary are not another presidential-vote condition. Section 302's March 20 caucus-notice date is separate. None receives blanket constitutional approval.

**Stevens, joined by Kennedy, Souter and Ginsburg, dissenting:** They agree that the original legal associational objection remains available, but would return the case for ordinary consideration of its actual factual basis, electoral burdens, precise state interests and feasible alternatives. Yee permits that legal refinement; the affidavit presents an issue to examine rather than a categorical loss of the claim. Norman and Anderson–Burdick require attention to real organizing burdens. Timmons's nonfusion holding and Reform Party's funding rule do not decide this retention condition, and nominal statutory access does not establish its actual cost. They neither find exclusive-local intent nor declare the condition unconstitutional, and they require no recognition, injunction or new election.
sections.Procedure After Action: Ordinary mandate follows affirmance. The reviewed summary judgment remains effective. No Supreme Court protection is inferred from the earlier agreed injunction described in the state proceedings, and no new filing, deadline, election, compulsory hearing or continuing injunction is ordered.
sections.Source Notes: The [First Circuit opinion, 173 F.3d 1](https://law.resource.org/pub/us/case/reporter/F3/173/173.F3d.1.98-1309.html), also [reported by OpenJurist](https://openjurist.org/173/f3d/1/maine-green-party-v-maine-secretary-of-state), supplies the competing accounts of preservation and the electoral history. The original summary-judgment papers are not independently reproduced here; the disputed factual premise is not resolved by their absence. The [official 1997 chapter 581](https://www.mainelegislature.org/ros/LOM/LOM118th/LOMPublic563-583-20.htm) and [chapter 436](https://www.mainelegislature.org/ros/LOM/LOM118th/LOM413to436-30.htm) supply the distinct current petition and notice provisions. May 20 is the scheduling date for this merits consideration; no separate Supreme Court docket number or argument date is established.

header: **Case and dockets:** California Dental Association v. Federal Trade Commission; No. 97-1625.

sections.Event:
California Dental Association v. Federal Trade Commission, No. 97-1625. Argued January 13, 1999; decided May 24, 1999. On certiorari to the Ninth Circuit, 128 F.3d 720, which affirmed and enforced the Commission's cease-and-desist order. The questions are whether the FTC Act reaches this nonprofit association organized to benefit for-profit dentists and whether the actual price- and quality-advertising restrictions received sufficient rule-of-reason analysis.

CDA's roughly 75% statewide membership, commercial benefits and enforcement are described in the appellate record. The ALJ found practical restrictions on low-fee descriptions, broad discounts and quality claims without individualized truthfulness review. The Commission relied on per se treatment of price restrictions and alternatively on abbreviated analysis; the Ninth Circuit rejected the per se basis but sustained abbreviated review of price and quality separately. The ALJ and Commission differed on market power. Those positions are distinct from a Supreme Court factual finding.
sections.Participation: All nine Justices participate at argument and decision: Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer.
sections.Public Action: The FTC's statutory coverage is sustained. The enforcement judgment is vacated and the case remanded for further proceedings.
sections.Judgment & Remedy:
| Judgment component | Disposition and vote | Supporting Justices | Opposing Justices | Remedy and scope |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FTC statutory coverage | Sustained, 9–0 | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer | — | Coverage is resolved; no final liability follows from it. |
| Price-advertising liability | Vacated and remanded, 5–4 | Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Scalia, Souter, Thomas | Stevens, Kennedy, Ginsburg, Breyer | The existing abbreviated analysis is insufficient; further restraint-sensitive consideration is required. |
| Quality-advertising liability | Vacated and remanded, 5–4 | Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Scalia, Souter, Thomas | Stevens, Kennedy, Ginsburg, Breyer | Same formal relief, with the distinct quality-information analysis below. |

The case returns through the Ninth Circuit. O'Connor, Scalia, Souter and Thomas would leave that court to decide whether it can assess the Commission's decision on the existing record or should return it for more extensive agency analysis and an enhanced record. Stone-Zsela would require the Commission itself to conduct the fuller inquiry. Neither institutional direction commands five votes. The common judgment finds neither final liability nor reasonableness and directs no damages or new sanction.
sections.Opinion Topology:
| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to judgment | Scope joined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court on statutory coverage | Souter | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer | Unanimous coverage determination | Complete coverage rule and limits. |
| Opinion of the Court on competitive analysis | Souter | Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Scalia, Thomas | Supports vacatur of both advertising components | Flexible inquiry and both insufficiency applications; no final liability. |
| Lead opinion's remedial allocation discussion | Souter | O'Connor, Scalia, Thomas | Supports vacatur and further proceedings | Ninth Circuit choice between existing-record assessment and further Commission analysis; four Justices only. |
| Concurrence in part and in the judgment | Stone-Zsela | No other Justice | Supports coverage and vacatur/remand | Joins coverage and competitive analysis; requires Commission inquiry instead of the four-Justice appellate choice. |
| Concurrence in part and dissent in part | Breyer | Stevens, Kennedy, Ginsburg | Joins coverage; would affirm liability | Complete alternative rule-of-reason assessment of price, quality, justification and practical effect. |
sections.Holdings:
### Coverage includes an association serving its members' commercial profit

**Holding and operative rule:** The FTC Act reaches a nonprofit professional association organized to carry on business for its members' profit when its activities confer proximate, substantial economic benefits on their for-profit operations. CDA satisfies that condition through its insurance, financing, commercial support and other member-business activities; nonprofit form, tax status and absence of distributions to the association do not eliminate the members'-profit branch of section 44.

**Authority:** Souter's coverage opinion, joined by all eight other Justices, directly controls this proposition.

**Controlling explanation:** The statutory alternative concerning members' profit would do little work if only the association's own earnings counted. CDA materially advances its members' commercial practices, so the outside suppliers' role does not make those benefits merely incidental. This application does not require exclusive devotion to member profit, a substantial percentage of total activity devoted to it, or proof that each member makes a net profit from membership. The connection must be real and proximate; professional education's presumed or incidental benefit alone is not held sufficient. The Court does not decide coverage of every charity, educational organization, nonprofit with an annual surplus, or commercial competitor without for-profit members. Ordinary statutory interpretation suffices, without deciding deference to the Commission's jurisdictional view. Section 45's sector exceptions remain; none is established for CDA. Neither professional status nor an unverified guideline's description of state law supplies immunity. Coverage authorizes inquiry, not condemnation.

### The inquiry must test the restraint's actual competitive tendency and material explanation

**Holding and operative rule:** An abbreviated rule-of-reason inquiry may suffice when experience and the restraint's actual character make its likely anticompetitive tendency sufficiently clear to assess both the restraint and its material competing explanation. Where professional-information disparities make those effects insufficiently obvious, fuller analysis fitted to the restraint is required; neither a fixed sequence of labels nor a complete industry or market-definition study is invariably compulsory.

**Authority:** Souter's competitive-analysis opinion, joined by Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Scalia and Thomas, supplies five direct joins for this rule and both applications below.

**Controlling explanation:** NCAA permits inquiry calibrated to an established competitive mechanism. Professional Engineers rejects the claim that competition itself is undesirable; it does not dispense with examining a plausible claim that a practice improves reliable comparison. Indiana Federation of Dentists permits direct analysis of an agreement withholding a desired service, but does not make every professional-information restriction identical to that agreement. Khan and NYNEX require attention to the actual restraint and mechanism without converting this horizontal association into a vertical arrangement. The FTC's concrete enforcement findings are adverse evidence, not a substitute for the missing analysis of information quality. The Court corrects legal sufficiency and does not reweigh supported findings under section 45(c), independently affirm every economic conclusion, or decide whether substantial evidence supports ultimate liability. It finds neither restraint reasonable and creates no professional immunity. Legitimate restraints on materially false or misleading advertising remain possible under their actual conditions; no categorical per se issue is independently decided.

### Price restrictions require more examination on this record

**Holding and operative rule:** The practical restrictions on fee descriptions and broad discount advertisements cannot be sustained on the abbreviated analysis employed here without adequately examining their asserted effect on the reliability of price comparison. Further inquiry must test the actual enforcement and claimed information benefits; the mere reduction of advertising does not settle the net competitive tendency.

**Authority:** The same five-Justice competitive-analysis opinion directly adopts this application.

**Controlling explanation:** Price communication ordinarily helps consumers compare and dentists compete. Bates recognizes that value while preserving legitimate deception controls. But an across-the-board discount without an intelligible baseline or scope may be unreliable, and a disclosure condition might improve comparison, obstruct it or do both. The reported restrictions on truthful descriptions and practically prohibitive disclosures remain serious evidence against CDA. Their existence alone does not adequately test whether these particular conditions improve reliable information before demanding empirical justification on the assumption of an already established harmful net tendency. This is no finding that every advertisement misleads, that every condition helps, or that CDA's explanation ultimately succeeds. The lower proceedings must perform the missing analysis without automatically adopting the ALJ's no-market-power conclusion, a local-share threshold or mandatory comprehensive market definition.

### Quality advertising is not equivalent to service output

**Holding and operative rule:** Quality-advertising restrictions whose effects depend on the reliability and verifiability of professional information require fuller consideration than equating fewer advertisements with a restriction of dental-service output. The actual conditions and competitive explanation must be assessed; possible effects on demand do not themselves establish a producer-imposed service-output restriction.

**Authority:** The same five-Justice opinion directly controls this distinct application.

**Controlling explanation:** Restricting useful quality information can impede service rivalry, yet patients may have difficulty verifying professional claims. A restraint addressing unverifiable or misleading claims may improve information. Bates recognizes that quality-claim problem, while Indiana Federation's established desired-service restraint provides no automatic answer to this different mechanism. The court below could not settle the matter merely by translating fewer advertisements into reduced dental output. The Court requires neither measured output decline in every antitrust case nor acceptance of a blanket ban. Supported enforcement against truthful information remains material. Fuller examination may condemn either or both restrictions, but the present analysis does not resolve their competitive explanation. The discontinued fear-allaying policy is not treated as a continuing restraint.
sections.Precedent Treatment:
- NCAA v. Board of Regents supplies flexible inquiry fitted to established competitive tendencies; it creates no compulsory full-market procedure.
- National Society of Professional Engineers v. United States remains a bar to defending restraints on the premise that competition itself is undesirable; an information-quality explanation must be tested on its actual competitive terms.
- FTC v. Indiana Federation of Dentists is distinguished at the level of the restraint and information mechanism; its direct-effects method and separation of supported findings from legal sufficiency remain.
- Bates v. State Bar of Arizona supplies the value of truthful price information and the distinct difficulty of unverifiable professional quality claims.
- State Oil Co. v. Khan retains its vertical maximum-price holding and horizontal distinctions; its attention to competitive mechanisms informs this inquiry without conferring immunity.
- NYNEX Corp. v. Discon retains its vertical supplier-substitution holding and distinct horizontal categories; labels or improper purpose do not replace analysis of the actual mechanism.
sections.Law After Decision: CDA falls within FTC coverage, but the existing price- and quality-advertising liability determination cannot stand on the analysis used. The required inquiry is proportionate to actual restraints and live competitive explanations. The Court establishes neither final liability nor professional immunity, and imposes no universal market-definition trial or required proof of measured service-output decline. Supported agency findings retain their statutory review status. No majority specifies whether the Ninth Circuit may complete the examination on the existing record or must direct Commission reconsideration.
sections.Separate Writings:
**Stone-Zsela, concurring in part and in the judgment:** The Chief joins coverage and the holdings requiring fuller, restraint-sensitive inquiry. The suppression of truthful comparison and the possible value of substantiation or discount disclosure must both be tested. He would direct the Commission itself to conduct that examination rather than permit the Ninth Circuit to complete it without Commission reconsideration. He requires no full market-definition trial in every case and grants no immunity for restraints on truthful, nonmisleading information.

**Souter's remedial discussion, joined by O'Connor, Scalia and Thomas:** These four would leave the Ninth Circuit to decide whether it can adequately assess the Commission's decision on the existing record or should return it for more extensive analysis and an enhanced record. Correcting legal sufficiency neither authorizes judicial reweighing of supported facts nor mandates a new administrative hearing. They make no ultimate substantial-evidence determination.

**Breyer, joined by Stevens, Kennedy and Ginsburg, concurring in part and dissenting in part:** They join coverage and the flexible rule-of-reason method but find the existing analysis sufficient for both categories. Actual enforcement, rather than the Code's facial aspiration against deception, suppresses low-fee descriptions and practically excludes broad discounts. Truthful discounts can inform consumers without listing every undiscounted service price. The supported quality restraint suppresses useful information without examining whether particular claims mislead; the mechanism is interference with communicating qualities and matching dentists to patients, not a finding that the number of procedures fell. Verification problems do not justify the actual breadth once those effects are shown.

On that showing CDA bears the burden of establishing an offsetting competitive benefit. A merely possible advantage does not require the Commission to refute every conceivable theory. These Justices find the inquiry and record adequately answer the reliability claim. Membership, entry barriers, economic benefits and dentists' interest in remaining members support practical effect; the statewide figure is not a finding of equal shares in every locality. Indiana Federation supplies direct-effects analysis and respect for supported Commission findings, while NCAA calibrates depth and Professional Engineers requires a competitive justification. They would affirm the existing enforcement judgment without a new order, sanction or damages. They endorse neither every disclosure restriction nor all professional advertising, and find no need to decide the Commission's per se alternative.
sections.Procedure After Action: The case returns to the Ninth Circuit with coverage resolved and the enforcement judgment vacated. Further proceedings must respect the five-Justice insufficiency holdings and section 45(c)'s treatment of supported findings. The four-Justice appellate option and the Chief's mandatory Commission direction remain separately stated, without either becoming a majority command. No final finding of reasonableness, liability, damages, market power or new sanction is entered.
sections.Source Notes: The [Ninth Circuit opinion, 128 F.3d 720](https://static.case.law/f3d/128/html/0720-01.html) supplies the reported administrative findings, enforcement practices and competing analyses. The governing text is [15 U.S.C. §44](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-1994-title15/html/USCODE-1994-title15-chap2-subchapI-sec44.htm) and [§45](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-1994-title15/html/USCODE-1994-title15-chap2-subchapI-sec45.htm). The [official reported chronology, 526 U.S. 756](https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/boundvolumes/526bv.pdf), supplies the argument and decision dates. The full administrative order and every advertisement are not independently reproduced; no unquoted order term, exact local share, state-law command or new advertisement finding is decided.

header: **Case and dockets:** Cleveland v. Policy Management Systems Corp.; No. 97-1008.

sections.Event:
Cleveland v. Policy Management Systems Corp., No. 97-1008. Argued February 24, 1999; decided May 24, 1999. On certiorari to the Fifth Circuit, 120 F.3d 513, which affirmed summary judgment on the federal ADA claim. The question concerns the effect of SSDI representations on proof that a person can perform essential job functions with or without reasonable accommodation.

Cleveland suffered a January 1994 stroke, sought benefits, returned to work in April, requested accommodation and was terminated in July. She asserts that she notified the SSA and withdrew the application on return; the employer concedes notice of return but disputes withdrawal or abandonment of disability representations. Later papers asserted disability and a September 1995 award treated it as continuous from January 1994. Cleveland asserts later worsening and earlier capacity with accommodation. The Fifth Circuit rejected a conclusive bar but imposed a rebuttable estoppel presumption, treating compatible claims as limited and highly unusual. The District Court separately dismissed the Texas claim without prejudice.
sections.Participation: All nine Justices participate at argument and decision: Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer.
sections.Public Action: The Fifth Circuit's federal ADA judgment is vacated, and the case is remanded for further proceedings under the ordinary statutory and evidentiary requirements.
sections.Judgment & Remedy:
**Vacated and remanded, 9–0.**

**Supporting:** Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer.

Cleveland must have an opportunity to offer a legally and factually sufficient explanation, and the employer may contest it. The lower courts must decide qualification, accommodation and any remaining defenses under the ADA. No compulsory trial, liability finding, award, benefits revision or automatic revival of the Texas claim follows.

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to judgment | Scope joined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court | Stevens | Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer | Unanimous vacatur and remand | Both holdings, their proof limits and ordinary remand. |

All nine join in full. No separate opinion is filed.
sections.Holdings:
### SSDI does not create an automatic bar or special adverse presumption under the ADA

**Holding and operative rule:** Applying for or receiving SSDI neither automatically estops an ADA plaintiff from proving qualification nor creates a special strong presumption against that proof. The statutes ask different questions, and qualification under the ADA still depends on the ability to perform the position's essential functions with or without reasonable accommodation.

**Authority:** Stevens's opinion, joined by all eight other Justices, controls this holding, the explanation requirement below and the bounded remand.

**Controlling explanation:** The ADA expressly includes reasonable accommodation in its qualification inquiry. SSDI's impairment, duration and vocational provisions do not conduct that same workplace-accommodation inquiry. Administrative listings and trial-work provisions, changes over time and properly alternative legal theories may also explain why the two claims coexist. Bragdon requires individual statutory analysis and founded proof; a label under one scheme cannot replace the elements of another. The Fifth Circuit recognized some of these distinctions but confined compatibility to a highly unusual class under its negative presumption. That presumption still treats the differing legal conclusions as ordinarily inconsistent and is unwarranted. The employer's concern about obtaining incompatible advantages is substantial, but ordinary evidentiary requirements address it without a label-based presumption. None of these possible explanations is a finding that Cleveland was qualified, that any accommodation was reasonable, or that discrimination occurred. The holding supplies no universal immunity from the consequences of contradictory historical facts and leaves general law governing purely factual contradictions and other statutes undisturbed.

### An apparent inconsistency still requires an adequate explanation

**Holding and operative rule:** An ADA plaintiff confronting an apparently inconsistent earlier total-disability representation must provide an explanation sufficient for a reasonable juror, accepting the earlier statement as true or as made in good faith, still to find that the plaintiff could perform the essential functions at the relevant time with or without reasonable accommodation. The plaintiff retains the ordinary qualification burden; good faith alone, a bare contradiction or a statutory label without an answer to the material factual inconsistency does not satisfy it.

**Authority:** The same unanimous Opinion of the Court directly adopts this requirement and its application.

**Controlling explanation:** Rule 56 asks whether the evidence permits a reasonable finding on the actual ADA element. Prior sworn assertions remain evidence. Statutory differences may explain an assertion about disability without erasing a contradictory statement about what the person actually could do. The explanation must address the relevant time, job functions and accommodation to the extent they create the apparent conflict. Cleveland's return to work, requested accommodations, asserted later worsening and the disputed status of her first application may matter, but the Court does not resolve their truth. The continuous-disability award also remains part of the record and must be addressed rather than assumed compatible. On remand both sides may present and contest the explanation, in sworn form where appropriate. A sufficient explanation permits ordinary assessment; it guarantees neither trial nor success. Summary judgment may again follow if the explanation is inadequate or another essential element is absent. The decision changes no benefits award, compels no unreasonable accommodation and makes no credibility finding.
sections.Precedent Treatment: Bragdon v. Abbott is applied at the shared level of individual statutory elements and founded objective proof. Its disability-definition and direct-threat holdings remain distinct and unchanged. Ordinary summary-judgment requirements remain; the Court does not adopt every lower-court rule concerning a later affidavit that contradicts earlier factual testimony.
sections.Law After Decision: SSDI application or receipt carries no special estoppel presumption in the ADA qualification inquiry. Apparent contradictions remain material evidence and require an adequate explanation under ordinary proof rules. Qualification, reasonable accommodation, discrimination and defenses retain their independent elements. This decision does not settle general judicial-estoppel doctrine for purely factual contradictions or other statutory relationships.
sections.Procedure After Action: The federal ADA judgment returns for consideration under the distinct statutory inquiries and adequate-explanation rule. Cleveland may offer the required explanation and the employer may challenge it; the lower courts decide whether the evidence suffices and address remaining properly available issues. No trial, damages, reinstatement or Social Security revision is ordered. The Texas dismissal without prejudice is not automatically restored as a pending federal claim.
sections.Source Notes: The complete [Fifth Circuit opinion, 120 F.3d 513](https://openjurist.org/120/f3d/513), supplies the actual rebuttable-presumption rule and reported chronology. The [official United States Reports, 526 U.S. 795–807](https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/boundvolumes/526bv.pdf), supplies the argument and decision dates. The relevant statutory provisions are 42 U.S.C. §§12111(8), 12112(a), 423(d)(1)(A) and 423(d)(2)(A). Original SSA papers are not independently reproduced; notification, withdrawal, worsening, functional capacity and reasonable accommodation remain matters for evidentiary assessment.

header: **Case and dockets:** Davis v. Monroe County Board of Education; No. 97-843.

sections.Event:
Davis v. Monroe County Board of Education, No. 97-843. Argued January 12, 1999; decided May 24, 1999. On certiorari to the en banc Eleventh Circuit, 120 F.3d 1390, which affirmed dismissal of the district's Title IX damages claim. The question is whether the funding recipient may be responsible for its own deliberate response to serious student-on-student sexual harassment within its substantial control.

A fifth-grade student allegedly endured repeated touching and sexual propositions by a classmate over several months. The child and her mother reportedly informed teachers and the principal; officials allegedly failed to protect her while the conduct continued and interfered with education. The harasser's later guilty plea is a procedural recital, not proof of every civil element or earlier institutional notice. The case concerns pleading sufficiency, not findings of recipient fault or damages.
sections.Participation: All nine Justices participate at argument and decision: Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer.
sections.Public Action: The judgment is reversed insofar as it affirms dismissal of the appealed Title IX damages claim against the district, and the case is remanded for ordinary further proceedings.
sections.Judgment & Remedy:
**Reversed and remanded, 6–3.**

**Supporting:** Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer.
**Opposing:** Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas.

The recipient claim may proceed under the stated conditions. Knowledge, culpability, control, sex-based educational deprivation, causation, compensable injury and any supported defense remain to be proved or decided. No compulsory trial, damages award, particular punishment, individual-capacity recovery or reopening of unrelated claims is ordered.

sections.Holdings:
### A school's own culpable response can support damages for controlled peer harassment

**Holding and operative rule:** A Title IX funding recipient may be liable for its own response to peer harassment because of sex when an official empowered to correct the harassment or its substantial danger has actual notice, the recipient substantially controls both the harasser and the relevant educational context, and deliberate and unreasonable disregard of that danger causally contributes to further harassment or vulnerability producing educational deprivation and compensable injury. A peer's attendance does not impute the peer's acts to the recipient; knowledge, culpability, control, sex-based discrimination and causal loss are independent requirements.

**Authority:** Ginsburg's Part I is joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Souter and Breyer; six direct joins establish this sufficient route.

**Controlling explanation:** Franklin permits compensation for proved intentional Title IX discrimination but leaves recipient responsibility to be established. Kinman's actual-notice route identifies a recipient's own deliberate disregard of a known educational danger. The Court extends that sufficient route to peer conduct where the school has substantial remedial control; it does not claim Kinman already decided peers. The school's knowing, culpable continuation of educational deprivation supplies the institutional wrong, answering the objection that a student cannot personally bind the funding recipient. Mere discipline authority or an ineffective result does not suffice. Actual notice must reach an official empowered to correct the danger; generic constructive notice, the harasser's own knowledge and technical policy noncompliance do not establish this route. A reasonable response is lawful even if harassment continues, and courts prescribe neither a selected punishment nor a victim's preferred remedy. Constitutional and statutory limits on discipline inform control and response. Gebser's school-delegated teacher authority does not transfer to classmates; its conjunctive teacher route and the other teacher holdings remain intact. The Court neither adopts ordinary negligence or general agency law nor rejects every distinct theory of direct official discrimination. Receipt of assistance remains separately necessary under NCAA v. Smith. Causal injury cannot be inferred solely from harassment predating legally sufficient recipient notice.

### Educational deprivation follows the contextual severe-or-pervasive standard

**Holding and operative rule:** The harassment must be sufficiently severe or pervasive to create an objectively abusive educational environment actually experienced as abusive and impair educational access or benefit in its full context. Sexually charged conduct or offense alone does not establish discrimination because of sex, the required educational harm or the independent institutional elements.

**Authority:** Ginsburg's Part II, joined by Stevens, O'Connor, Souter and Breyer, directly controls with five votes. Stone-Zsela does not join this disjunctive threshold; no combination of separate rationales is needed for its authority.

**Controlling explanation:** Kinman adopted severe-or-pervasive, objectively abusive and actually experienced educational harassment without mandatory psychiatric injury, measurable grade loss or a rigid list of factors. Its reliance on Meritor and Harris preserves attention to welcome, objective and experienced abuse, and the actual setting. The peer relationship affects the contextual application and recipient-control inquiry; it does not silently replace the substantive standard with a requirement that conduct be both severe and pervasive. Age, relationship, educational setting and actual effect may matter without becoming a mandatory checklist. Neither physical exclusion nor total loss of schooling is invariably required, and no one proxy is sufficient by itself. Ordinary teasing or offense fails without the substantive and institutional requirements. No universal rule determines whether one incident always suffices or never can. These allegations involve repeated touching and propositions over months with educational interference, a materially different claimed environment. The Court decides no ultimate fact and does not treat every unwelcome interaction as actionable discrimination.

### The pleaded recipient claim warrants ordinary further proceedings

**Holding and operative rule:** Allegations of repeated school-setting harassment, reports including to the principal, continued conduct, deliberately inadequate protection and resulting educational interference state a claim for examination under the sufficient recipient-fault route. The categorical dismissal must be reversed, but an absent element, reasonable response, inadequate control or notice, missing causation or a supported defense may defeat recovery on the developed record.

**Authority:** Part III is joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer; six directly support this allegation-stage application and remedy.

**Controlling explanation:** The alleged response concerns the district's own use of authority after reports of a known danger, rather than automatic responsibility for the classmate. The asserted repeated abuse and educational disruption permit the necessary elements to be tested. Allegations that reports reached the principal do not finally establish every official's corrective power, knowledge or opportunity; the criminal plea supplies no earlier notice or complete causal showing. The plaintiff must prove the institutional and substantive conditions, including postnotice causal injury. Existing compensation principles therefore require ordinary further adjudication, not immediate damages or judicial control of discipline. No compulsory trial follows if ordinary procedure establishes a missing element or valid defense. The decision reaches only the appealed district Title IX claim and leaves unrelated and individual claims outside the mandate.
sections.Precedent Treatment:
- Franklin v. Gwinnett County Public Schools is applied to available compensation for proved intentional discrimination, with recipient responsibility, causation and loss still distinct.
- Kinman v. Omaha Public School District is extended at its sufficient actual-notice/culpable-disregard route to substantially controlled peer conduct. Its severe-or-pervasive contextual educational-harm standard remains; the peer extension is stated expressly.
- Gebser v. Lago Vista Independent School District retains the limited teacher-authority-plus-recipient-fault conjunction and its rejection of exclusivity in teacher cases. Neither delegated teacher power nor that complete route is imputed to peers.
- NCAA v. Smith preserves the distinct federal-assistance recipient requirement; economic connection or control alone does not establish receipt.
- Meritor Savings Bank v. Vinson informs the distinction between participation and welcome through Kinman without importing employment attribution wholesale.
- Harris v. Forklift Systems informs the contextual objective-and-experienced abuse inquiry through Kinman, without mandatory psychiatric injury or any indispensable factor.
- Pennhurst State School and Hospital v. Halderman retains its funding-notice principle; the controlling recipient-own-wrong route concerns intentional educational discrimination, not automatic liability for a third party.
sections.Law After Decision: A funding recipient's own actually informed, deliberately unreasonable response to peer harassment within substantial control can support damages when all independent discrimination, educational-harm and causal-injury elements are established. The controlling environment threshold remains severe or pervasive, objectively abusive and actually experienced as abusive, with impaired educational access or benefit. Teacher-attribution rules remain separately bounded. Ordinary negligence, policy breach, unsuccessful reasonable correction and peer attendance alone do not establish liability. The Chief's separate reporting-failure extension does not become a controlling peer rule, and no complete alternative-attribution or defense code is decided.
sections.Separate Writings:
**Stone-Zsela, concurring in part and in the judgment:** The Chief joins the actual-notice recipient-fault route and the reversal on these allegations. The school is answerable for its own deliberately indifferent failure to use available authority after reliable notice, with meaningful control, clearly inadequate response, sex-based educational deprivation and causal injury independently proved. Kinman's sufficient notice route remains available, while Gebser's teacher authority cannot simply be attributed to a classmate. He would require severe, pervasive and objectively offensive peer harassment depriving the victim of equal educational access, and therefore withholds assent from the Court's severe-or-pervasive threshold. He additionally would recognize the recipient's willfully blind, deliberately indifferent reporting failure causing continuation as a sufficient institutional ground. That proposed reporting-failure extension is his separate position, not the Court's peer rule. Neither misconduct nor negligent supervision alone suffices; officials retain disciplinary discretion so long as the response is not deliberately indifferent. He requires no particular punishment and makes no liability finding.

**Kennedy, joined by Scalia and Thomas, dissenting:** They would affirm the appealed peer-harassment dismissal because Title IX's funding condition does not sufficiently establish this institutional attribution. Franklin makes compensation available after recipient discrimination is shown; it does not identify the recipient's wrong. Kinman concerned a teacher, and Gebser's additional route still requires materially enabling delegated teacher authority. A nonagent pupil does not have that link. These Justices address the Court's own-response theory directly: disciplinary power and knowing nonresponse to a student's discrimination do not, on their view, supply the necessary statutory duty or clear funding notice. Legal limits on school control and the breadth of the proposed obligation reinforce the objection. They neither find the allegations false nor approve the conduct. A supported claim that school officials themselves enforce rules differently because of sex remains distinct; they decide no such new claim. Existing teacher law and remedies for established recipient discrimination remain intact.
sections.Procedure After Action: The appealed Title IX dismissal is reversed and the case returns for ordinary proceedings under the controlling recipient and educational-harm rules. The lower courts determine the actual facts, elements, supported defenses and any compensable injury. No damages, compulsory trial, disciplinary measure, reopening of unrelated claims or additional Supreme Court date is directed.
sections.Source Notes: The reported pleading posture, argument and decision dates appear in the [official United States Reports, 526 U.S. 629–686](https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/boundvolumes/526bv.pdf), and the judgment below is 120 F.3d 1390. Exact warnings, each official's power, grievance efficacy and postnotice causal events remain allegation-stage matters; no original filing or complete evidentiary record is represented as a judicial finding. Title IX's 20 U.S.C. §1681(a) prohibition, the existing recipient requirement and the stated limits govern the claim.

header: **Case and dockets:** Hanlon v. Berger; No. 97-1927.

sections.Event:
Hanlon v. Berger, No. 97-1927. Argued March 24, 1999; decided May 24, 1999, on certiorari to the Ninth Circuit's judgment in Berger v. Hanlon, 129 F.3d 505. The reviewed question concerns federal officials' introduction of a nonassisting media crew during the March 1993 ranch search and their personal qualified immunity.

The March 18 warrant authorized a search of the ranch and appurtenant structures for wildlife-offense evidence but excluded the residence. A March 11 media agreement preceded the planned search during the week of March 22. On the Bergers' favorable summary-judgment account, agents and CNN personnel cooperated in observation and recording, with equipment on official vehicles. Agent Scrafford initially entered the home by consent while carrying an undisclosed media-owned microphone; later entries, consent and a residential search are disputed. Footage and home recordings were broadcast. Evidence places filmed outbuildings near the home with a guard dog; it does not classify every place on the 75,000-acre ranch.

The lower opinion separately addressed media defendants, joint action, statutory and tort claims and publication relief. Those rulings are not before the Court merely because they appear in the same reported judgment.
sections.Participation: All nine Justices participate at argument and decision: Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer.
sections.Public Action: The judgment is vacated only insofar as it determines the reviewed federal officials' media-participation claim, and the case is remanded with the qualified-immunity direction and limits below.
sections.Judgment & Remedy:
| Judgment component | Disposition and vote | Supporting Justices | Opposing or differently aligned Justices | Remedy and scope |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Reviewed federal-official media-participation determination | Limited vacatur and remand, 8–1 | Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer | Stone-Zsela would affirm denial of immunity and remand | Only this reviewed component is vacated; distinct unreviewed claims are untouched. |
| Personal immunity on the reviewed media-participation theory | Immunity required, 7–2 | O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer | Stone-Zsela and Stevens oppose immunity for supported unauthorized physical media intrusion into protected space | Apply immunity on the reviewed accompaniment, observation and recording enterprise theory, without immunizing every distinct residential entry or search. |

Stevens accepts limited vacatur to separate actual spaces and acts, but would preserve denial of immunity for the protected-space physical intrusion. The Chief's preferred affirmance is distinct. Neither the eight-vote appellate result nor the seven-vote immunity direction decides damages, each official's acts, private-media liability or every recording's constitutional status.

| Concurrence in part and dissent in part | Stevens | No other Justice | Accepts limited vacatur; opposes physical-entry immunity | Joins Parts I–II and IV, preserving denial of immunity for supported protected-space physical intrusion. |
